On the Structural Foundations of Signature Volatility Models: Existence, Arbitrage, Completeness, and the Hedging-Error Decomposition

Akmal Xodarev Affiliation: Independent Researcher Affiliation: ORCID: 0009-0000-5318-7284 Email: xodarevakmal@gmail.com Affiliation: Tashkent, Uzbekistan
First version: February 8, 2026
This version: May 17, 2026
Abstract

We establish four structural results for signature volatility models. First, we prove global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to the signature stochastic differential equation d​St=St​⟨ℓ,W^t⟩​d​BtdS_{t}=S_{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\,dB_{t} on the weighted tensor algebra space TwT_{w}, identifying the admissibility class through the summability condition H1 and the exponential-integrability condition H3 needed for the square-integrable stochastic-exponential construction. Second, we establish the asset-pricing part on the natural filtration of the prolonged signature and separate it from the transform non-explosion part: H3 makes the reference-measure stochastic exponential a true martingale, hence yields NFLVR, while global solvability of the associated infinite-dimensional Riccati equation is the additional condition equivalent to absence of explosion for finite signature transforms. Third, we characterise market completeness on the price filtration in terms of the density of the truncated signature span span⁡{⟨eI,W^T⟩:|I|≤N}\operatorname{span}\{\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{T}\right\rangle:|I|\leq N\} inside L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}), and we identify the minimal such truncation NN, which we name the price-filtration completeness depth of the model. Fourth, we derive the hedging-error decomposition X=𝔼ℚ​[X]+∫0THs​d​Ss+εTX=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X]+\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\,dS_{s}+\varepsilon_{T} for square-integrable payoffs, in which the residual is expanded through the Gram projection of signature components beyond the completeness depth and bounded by a model-dependent projection error. The four results are tied together by an architectural identity: the admissible weighted tensor algebra on which the stochastic exponential is a true martingale and finite signature transforms do not explode is the natural valuation cell of a signature SDE. The proofs are self-contained except for standard results from rough path theory, stochastic integration, and quadratic hedging, which are recalled in the appendices.

Keywords. Signature SDE; weighted tensor algebra; asset-pricing theorem; market completeness; hedging-error decomposition; rough volatility.

MSC 2020 classification. Primary: 91G20, 91G30. Secondary: 60H05, 60H10, 60G44.

JEL classification. C58, G13.

1 Introduction

1.1 The structural gap

The signature volatility literature has produced, in the three years from 2022 to 2025, a body of applied results in calibration and pricing that rests on a structural foundation built only piecewise. Cuchiero et al. (2025a) construct joint SPX–VIX calibration with signature-based models and exploit affine structure of augmented signatures for pricing. Abi Jaber and Gérard (2025) derive Fourier pricing and quadratic hedging formulas under signature volatility models through an infinite-dimensional Riccati representation. Cuchiero and Möller (2025) introduce signature methods in stochastic portfolio theory and obtain tractable optimisation problems for path-functional portfolios. Cuchiero et al. (2025b) prove universal approximation for functions of càdlàg paths and define Lévy-type signature models. Each of these works either assumes, or proves under restrictive hypotheses, four structural facts: well-posedness of the signature SDE, the true martingale property of its stochastic exponential, the existence of an equivalent local martingale measure and of a hedging strategy.

The structural theorems on which these assumptions rest exist in piecewise form. Cuchiero et al. (2023) establish the affine and polynomial structure of the prolonged signature process on the extended tensor algebra and derive Riccati and linear ODEs for Fourier–Laplace transforms under integrability hypotheses. Abi Jaber et al. (2025) prove, in the one-dimensional signature-volatility model, that the discounted price process is a true martingale precisely in the odd-order negative-correlation regime, and characterise the complementary finite-time explosion of exponential moments of the integrated variance. The unification into a single chain of four structural theorems does not yet exist. For signature volatility models, the present work supplies the structural analogue of Delbaen and Schachermayer (1994) for general semimartingale models and of Filipović and Larsson (2016) for polynomial diffusions.

1.2 The contribution

Throughout, the labels Theorem A, Theorem B, Theorem C, Theorem D refer to Theorems 3.1, 4.2, 5.3, and 6.3 respectively; each is stated in the section bearing the corresponding letter and is preceded by the auxiliary lemma its proof uses.

Theorem A establishes global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to the signature stochastic differential equation on the weighted tensor algebra space TwT_{w}. Given a parameter ℓ\ell in the dual of TwT_{w} satisfying the compatibility condition ∑n≥0w⁡(n)​|ℓn|2<∞\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}<\infty, the equation d​St=St​⟨ℓ,W^t⟩​d​BtdS_{t}=S_{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\,dB_{t} admits a unique strong solution on [0,T][0,T], strictly positive almost surely. The admissible weights are characterised by the summability condition together with the geometric growth condition H2, and the square-integrable solution class is obtained under the exponential-integrability condition H3. The proof, given in Section 3, constructs the solution as the Doléans–Dade stochastic exponential of the signature-volatility martingale and proves uniqueness by localisation. Theorem A does not assert a pointwise maximal weight, and Section 3.7 shows that the summability condition cannot be removed from the weighted estimates.

Theorem B establishes the asset-pricing theorem on the natural filtration of the prolonged signature and, separately, the transform non-explosion theorem governed by the Riccati flow. Under H1–H3 the reference measure itself is already an equivalent true-martingale measure: S=s0​ℰ​(M)S=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M) with M=∫⟨ℓ,W^⟩​𝑑BM=\int\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}\right\rangle\,dB, and H3 verifies Novikov and the required uniform-integrability estimates. Thus NFLVR follows directly from Delbaen–Schachermayer under ℙ\mathbb{P}. The Riccati equation is not used to manufacture an equivalent martingale measure; it is the transform-side condition that controls finite signature Fourier–Laplace transforms. The shuffle identity ⟨ℓ,W^⟩2=⟨ℓ⊔⁣⊔ℓ,W^⟩\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}\right\rangle^{2}=\left\langle\ell\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}\ell,\widehat{W}\right\rangle expresses the quadratic-variation integrand of MM as a second-order signature contraction, while the actual Riccati vector field is written below through the finite-level generator and its carre-du-champ constants. Theorem B therefore does not assert that NFLVR is equivalent to global Riccati solvability; Section 4 explains why that stronger assertion is not part of the theorem: Riccati solvability is a transform-domain hypothesis, not an asset-pricing hypothesis.

Theorem C characterises market completeness on the price filtration. The market formed by the underlying SS together with a finite collection of European vanilla options {Ci}i=1k\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k} on SS is complete with respect to ℱTS\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T} if and only if the closed truncated signature span, restricted to L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}), is dense in L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) for some finite NN, depending only on the weight ww and on the parameter ℓ\ell. The minimal such NN is named the price-filtration completeness depth NS∗​(ℓ,w)N^{\ast}_{S}(\ell,w). The proof combines the Galtchouk–Kunita–Watanabe projection with the market completion theorem of Davis and Obłój (2008), applied only to price-filtration claims. Theorem C does not assert that finite completeness depth on the full Brownian signature filtration is generic; rough Bergomi has infinite price-filtration completeness depth, as is shown in Section 7.4.

Theorem D derives the hedging-error decomposition. For every X∈L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)X\in L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) there exists a unique decomposition X=𝔼ℚ​[X]+∫0THs​d​Ss+εTX=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X]+\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\,dS_{s}+\varepsilon_{T} where HH is the Galtchouk–Kunita–Watanabe projection and εT\varepsilon_{T} is the residual orthogonal to stochastic integrals against SS. The residual εT\varepsilon_{T} admits a qualitative L2L^{2} expansion in the signature components of multi-index length exceeding the completeness depth, with coefficients determined by the finite Gram normal equations of the quotient signature family. A quantitative weight-tail bound is asserted only for payoffs in the weighted-signature class 𝒲w​(ℱTS,ℚ)\mathcal{W}_{w}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}), where the required coefficient decay is part of the hypothesis. Theorem D does not provide a constructive hedging algorithm, only the structural decomposition; algorithmic implementations are the subject of Abi Jaber and Gérard (2025).

1.3 The architectural identity

The four theorems are tied together by a single architectural identity: the admissible weighted tensor algebra on which the stochastic exponential is a true martingale and on which the finite signature transforms do not explode is the natural valuation cell of the model. The algebra is TwT_{w}, where the weight ww belongs to the admissible class determined by H1 and H2. The martingale part of the cell is supplied by Theorem A and H3. The transform part is the requirement that ∂tut=ℛ⁡(ut)\partial_{t}u_{t}=\mathcal{R}(u_{t}) has a global solution on [0,T][0,T] for the finitely supported transform directions under consideration. Keeping these two requirements distinct is necessary: H1–H3 can imply NFLVR while the transform Riccati flow still explodes in directions outside the finite transform domain.

1.4 Relation to the literature

Cuchiero et al. (2023), “Signature SDEs from an affine and polynomial perspective”, established the affine and polynomial structure of the prolonged signature process on the extended tensor algebra and derived Riccati and linear ODEs for Fourier–Laplace transforms under integrability hypotheses. Their current formulation covers characteristics that are linear maps of the signature on the extended tensor algebra. The present Theorem A works in the weighted Banach algebra TwT_{w}, identifies the sharp summability class through H1, and proves global existence under H1–H3. The cited affine-polynomial theory does not by itself supply the square-integrable stochastic-exponential construction used here for the asset-pricing theorem.

Abi Jaber et al. (2025), “Martingale property and moment explosions in signature volatility models”, proved that, in the one-dimensional signature-volatility model, the discounted price process is a true martingale if and only if the order of the linear form in the signature parameter is odd and the spot–volatility correlation is negative. Outside this regime, the moment-generating function of the integrated variance explodes in finite time. The present Theorem B separates this issue into its two structural components on the prolonged signature filtration: the martingale/NFLVR conclusion supplied by H3, and the transform non-explosion conclusion supplied by the Riccati lifetime. The explosion-time analysis of Abi Jaber, Gassiat and Sotnikov is represented by the lifetime of the corresponding Riccati solution in the one-dimensional reduction. The one-dimensional criterion does not address completeness or the GKW residual on the price filtration, which are handled separately in Theorems C and D.

Abi Jaber and Gérard (2025), “Signature volatility models: pricing and hedging with Fourier”, supplied an algorithmic framework for pricing and hedging via Fourier methods, under the standing assumption of well-posedness and tractable Laplace transform. The present Theorems C and D supply the structural theorems under which their algorithm is well-posed: the price-filtration completeness depth identifies the minimal static completion level for replicability, and the residual decomposition bounds the unhedgeable error. Their Fourier framework gives algorithms after the structural hypotheses are granted; the present paper isolates the hypotheses and proves the corresponding projection statements.

1.5 Proof dependencies

The four theorems are ordered so that each proof uses only the analytic structure already established. Theorem 3.1 supplies the stochastic exponential, strict positivity, and L2L^{2} control. Theorem 4.2 uses these estimates first to obtain the reference-measure martingale and NFLVR conclusion, and then to state the separate Riccati transform non-explosion criterion. Theorem 5.3 uses the equivalent martingale measure and the signature filtration identity to state completeness on ℱTS\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T} rather than on the full Brownian filtration. Theorem 6.3 uses the completeness depth from Theorem 5.3 as the boundary separating replicated coordinates from residual coordinates.

There are two places where the grading of the tensor algebra is essential. The first is the estimate

|⟨ℓ,W^t⟩|≤‖ℓ‖2,w​‖W^t‖2,w−1,\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}\left\lVert\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{2,w^{-1}},

which converts summability of the parameter into integrability of the volatility functional. The second is the shuffle identity

⟨eI,W^T⟩​⟨eJ,W^T⟩=⟨eI⊔⁣⊔eJ,W^T⟩,\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{T}\right\rangle\left\langle e_{J},\widehat{W}_{T}\right\rangle=\left\langle e_{I}\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}e_{J},\widehat{W}_{T}\right\rangle,

which is responsible for both the Riccati closure and the Gram-system formula in the hedging-error theorem. Thus the algebraic and probabilistic arguments are not separate: the same graded multiplication controls stochastic exponentials, transform equations, and residual projections.

The formulation also separates three filtrations that must not be conflated. The Brownian filtration ℱW\mathcal{F}^{W} equals the prolonged-signature filtration ℱW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}, because the time-augmented signature recovers the Brownian path. The price filtration ℱS\mathcal{F}^{S} is generally smaller. The static option filtration at maturity is smaller again unless the option family is dense in the relevant terminal payoff space. Completeness in this paper is therefore not a statement about recovering all Brownian randomness; it is a statement about whether the dynamically traded price, together with the specified static completion, spans the square-integrable claims measurable with respect to the price filtration.

This dependency structure is the reason for the order of the manuscript. A proof of completeness without Theorem 4.2 would lack the martingale measure needed for the Hilbert-space projection. A proof of the hedging-error decomposition without Theorem 5.3 would have no canonical depth at which to split the signature coordinates. A proof of the Riccati transform statement without Theorem 3.1 would have no true stochastic exponential estimates available for the transform domain. The statements are consequently presented as a chain rather than as four independent propositions.

1.6 Organisation of the paper

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 sets up notation, the weighted tensor algebra, and the signature SDE. Section 3 proves Theorem A. Section 4 proves Theorem B. Section 5 proves Theorem C. Section 6 proves Theorem D. Section 7 collects examples: Black–Scholes, first-order Brownian-driven volatility, Heston, rough Bergomi, Quintic OU, and Guyon–Lekeufack path-dependent volatility, each cast as a signature SDE with explicit completeness depth. Section 8 closes with open problems. Three appendices recall results from rough path theory, the explicit form of the Riccati operator, and the Galtchouk–Kunita–Watanabe projection.

2 Notation and the weighted tensor algebra

2.1 The free tensor algebra over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}

Throughout this paper we fix a finite time horizon T>0T>0 and a complete probability space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) supporting a dd-dimensional standard Brownian motion WW.

Definition 2.1 (Free tensor algebra).

The free tensor algebra over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is

T⁡(ℝd)=⨁n≥0(ℝd)⊗n,(ℝd)⊗0=ℝ.T(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{\otimes n},\qquad(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{\otimes 0}=\mathbb{R}.

The canonical basis is denoted by {eI}\{e_{I}\}, where I=(i1,…,in)I=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}) is a multi-index with ik∈{1,…,d}i_{k}\in\{1,\ldots,d\}, |I|=n|I|=n, and e∅=1e_{\emptyset}=1.

Definition 2.2 (Concatenation, shuffle, Hopf structure).

Concatenation is the associative non-commutative product determined by eI⋅eJ=eI​Je_{I}\cdot e_{J}=e_{IJ}. The shuffle product eI⊔⁣⊔eJe_{I}\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}e_{J} is the commutative associative product obtained by summing over all order-preserving interlacings of II and JJ. The Hopf algebra antipode is A⁡(ei1​…​in)=(−1)n​ein​…​i1A(e_{i_{1}\ldots i_{n}})=(-1)^{n}e_{i_{n}\ldots i_{1}}.

Definition 2.3 (Extended tensor algebra).

The extended tensor algebra is

T⁡((ℝd))=∏n≥0(ℝd)⊗n.T((\mathbb{R}^{d}))=\prod_{n\geq 0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{\otimes n}.

Elements of T⁡((ℝd))T((\mathbb{R}^{d})) are formal series whose homogeneous levels need not vanish beyond finite degree.

The algebraic identities used below are the standard identities of the shuffle Hopf algebra; see Reutenauer (1993, Chapters 1 and 6) and Friz and Victoir (2010, Chapter 2).

2.2 The signature of a path

Definition 2.4 (Signature of a smooth path).

Let X:[0,T]→ℝdX:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be continuous and of bounded variation. Its signature over [0,t][0,t] is

𝐗t=∑n≥0∑|I|=neI∫0<t1<⋯<tn<tdXt1i1⋯dXtnin∈T((ℝd)).\mathbf{X}_{t}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{|I|=n}e_{I}\int_{0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}<t}dX^{i_{1}}_{t_{1}}\cdots dX^{i_{n}}_{t_{n}}\in T((\mathbb{R}^{d})).
Definition 2.5 (Stratonovich signature for semimartingales).

For a continuous semimartingale, the same formula defines the Stratonovich signature when the iterated integrals are interpreted in the Stratonovich sense. The prolonged signature W^t\widehat{W}_{t} is the signature of the time-augmented Brownian motion W^t=(t,Wt1,…,Wtd)\widehat{W}_{t}=(t,W^{1}_{t},\ldots,W^{d}_{t}).

Theorem 2.6 (Chen identity).

For 0≤s≤t≤T0\leq s\leq t\leq T,

W^0,t=W^0,s⊗W^s,t.\widehat{W}_{0,t}=\widehat{W}_{0,s}\otimes\widehat{W}_{s,t}.
Proof.

The identity follows by decomposing each simplex 0<u1<⋯<un<t0<u_{1}<\cdots<u_{n}<t according to the last integration time below ss and the first integration time above ss. The resulting ordered interlacings are precisely the tensor-concatenation components of W^0,s⊗W^s,t\widehat{W}_{0,s}\otimes\widehat{W}_{s,t}; see Chen (1977) and Friz and Victoir (2010, Chapter 2). ∎

Theorem 2.7 (Shuffle identity).

For multi-indices I,JI,J and every bounded variation path, and by Stratonovich extension for continuous semimartingales,

⟨eI,𝐗t⟩​⟨eJ,𝐗t⟩=⟨eI⊔⁣⊔eJ,𝐗t⟩.\left\langle e_{I},\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\rangle\left\langle e_{J},\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\rangle=\left\langle e_{I}\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}e_{J},\mathbf{X}_{t}\right\rangle.
Proof.

The product of the two iterated integrals is an integral over the product of two simplices. The product domain decomposes into disjoint ordered simplices indexed by shuffles of II and JJ. This gives the stated identity; see Reutenauer (1993, Chapters 1 and 6). ∎

Theorem 2.8 (Signature uniqueness).

The signature map on continuous semimartingale paths is injective up to tree-like equivalence. In particular, the augmented natural filtration of the prolonged signature satisfies ℱtW^=ℱtW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}=\mathcal{F}^{W}_{t}.

Proof.

The uniqueness statement is the rough-path uniqueness theorem of Boedihardjo et al. (2016). The equality of filtrations follows because the first level of the time-augmented signature recovers (t,Wt)(t,W_{t}) and the full signature is measurable with respect to the path of WW up to time tt. ∎

2.3 The weighted tensor algebra

Definition 2.9 (Weight).

A weight is a map w:ℕ→(0,∞)w:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty) such that w⁡(0)=1w(0)=1 and ww is increasing.

Definition 2.10 (Weighted tensor algebra).

For a weight ww, define

Tw={a=(an)n≥0∈T⁡((ℝd)):‖a‖w:=∑n≥0w⁡(n)​|an|(ℝd)⊗n<∞}.T_{w}=\left\{a=(a_{n})_{n\geq 0}\in T((\mathbb{R}^{d})):\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}:=\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\left\lvert a_{n}\right\rvert_{(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{\otimes n}}<\infty\right\}.
Proposition 2.11 (Banach algebra property).

If the weight satisfies w⁡(m+n)≤Cw​w​(m)​w​(n)w(m+n)\leq C_{w}w(m)w(n) for some Cw≥1C_{w}\geq 1, then TwT_{w} is a Banach algebra under concatenation and

‖a⊗b‖w≤Cw​‖a‖w​‖b‖w.\left\lVert a\otimes b\right\rVert_{w}\leq C_{w}\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{w}.
Proof.

Completeness follows from completeness of the weighted ℓ1\ell^{1} sum of the finite-dimensional tensor levels. For a,b∈Twa,b\in T_{w}, the homogeneous component of a⊗ba\otimes b at level nn equals ∑k=0nak⊗bn−k\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}\otimes b_{n-k}, hence

‖a⊗b‖w≤∑n≥0w⁡(n)​∑k=0n|ak|​|bn−k|.\left\lVert a\otimes b\right\rVert_{w}\leq\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left\lvert a_{k}\right\rvert\left\lvert b_{n-k}\right\rvert.

Submultiplicativity gives w⁡(n)=w⁡(k+(n−k))≤Cw​w​(k)​w​(n−k)w(n)=w(k+(n-k))\leq C_{w}w(k)w(n-k) for every 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n. Therefore

‖a⊗b‖w≤Cw​∑k≥0w⁡(k)​|ak|​∑j≥0w⁡(j)​|bj|=Cw​‖a‖w​‖b‖w.\left\lVert a\otimes b\right\rVert_{w}\leq C_{w}\sum_{k\geq 0}w(k)\left\lvert a_{k}\right\rvert\sum_{j\geq 0}w(j)\left\lvert b_{j}\right\rvert=C_{w}\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{w}.

∎

Proposition 2.12 (Signature moment bound).

For every T>0T>0, every p<∞p<\infty, and every weight ww with w⁡(n)≤rnw(n)\leq r^{n} for some r>0r>0, there exists M⁡(T,p,r)<∞M(T,p,r)<\infty such that

𝔼​‖W^t‖wp≤M⁡(T,p,r),t≤T.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{w}^{p}\leq M(T,p,r),\qquad t\leq T.
Proof.

The Brownian signature moment estimate recalled in Appendix A gives factorial decay in the tensor level. Exponential growth of the weight is therefore summable against the Brownian simplex-factor decay. Minkowski’s inequality and Gaussian moment estimates give the asserted uniform ppth moment bound. ∎

Remark 2.13 (Explicit moment control).

The proof of Proposition 2.12 gives an explicit bound of the form

M⁡(T,p,r)≤Cp,d​exp⁡{Cp,d​r2​T},M(T,p,r)\leq C_{p,d}\exp\{C_{p,d}r^{2}T\},

with constants depending only on the displayed parameters and on the dimension. The precise numerical value is immaterial below; only the uniformity in t≤Tt\leq T and the exponential dependence on the weight-growth parameter are used in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4.

Definition 2.14 (Dual space).

The continuous dual Tw∗T_{w}^{\ast} is identified with formal series ℓ=(ℓn)n≥0\ell=(\ell_{n})_{n\geq 0} such that

‖ℓ‖Tw∗:=supn≥0|ℓn|w⁡(n)<∞.\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{T_{w}^{\ast}}:=\sup_{n\geq 0}\frac{\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert}{w(n)}<\infty.

The duality pairing with a∈Twa\in T_{w} is

⟨ℓ,a⟩:=∑n≥0⟨ℓn,an⟩,\left\langle\ell,a\right\rangle:=\sum_{n\geq 0}\left\langle\ell_{n},a_{n}\right\rangle,

and |⟨ℓ,a⟩|≤‖ℓ‖Tw∗​‖a‖w\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,a\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{T_{w}^{\ast}}\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}.

For estimates involving H1 we also use the auxiliary weighted Hilbert norm

‖ℓ‖2,w2:=∑n≥0w⁡(n)​|ℓn|2,‖a‖2,w−12:=∑n≥0w​(n)−1​|an|2.\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}^{2}:=\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2},\qquad\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{2,w^{-1}}^{2}:=\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)^{-1}\left\lvert a_{n}\right\rvert^{2}.

The Cauchy–Schwarz estimate |⟨ℓ,a⟩|≤‖ℓ‖2,w​‖a‖2,w−1\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,a\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{2,w^{-1}} is used throughout Section 3.

2.4 Signature SDEs

Definition 2.15 (Signature SDE).

Given ℓ∈Tw∗\ell\in T_{w}^{\ast}, s0>0s_{0}>0, and a fixed unit vector η∈ℝd\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the signature SDE on TwT_{w} is

d​St=St​⟨ℓ,W^t⟩​d​Bt,S0=s0,dS_{t}=S_{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\,dB_{t},\qquad S_{0}=s_{0},

where Bt=∫0tη⋅d​WsB_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\eta\cdot dW_{s} is the ℱW\mathcal{F}^{W}-Brownian motion driven by WW in the direction η\eta. The Brownian motion BB driving the price SDE may therefore be correlated with the underlying dd-dimensional Brownian motion WW through the fixed unit vector η\eta; the special case η=e1\eta=e_{1} gives the canonical one-factor embedding.

Definition 2.16 (Signature filtration).

The filtration ℱtW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t} is the augmented natural filtration of W^\widehat{W}. By Theorem 2.8, ℱtW^=ℱtW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}=\mathcal{F}^{W}_{t}.

Definition 2.17 (Admissible strategies).

A predictable process HH is SS-admissible if

∫0T|Hs|2​Ss2​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s<∞a.s.\int_{0}^{T}|H_{s}|^{2}S_{s}^{2}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds<\infty\quad\text{a.s.}

The corresponding wealth process is Vt=V0+∫0tHs​d​SsV_{t}=V_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}H_{s}\,dS_{s}.

2.5 The Riccati operator

Definition 2.18 (Riccati operator).

For each finite truncation level NN, let 𝒜Nℓ\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell} denote the generator of the stopped finite-coordinate prolonged-signature system after the martingale price dynamics have been imposed. For coordinate functions YI​(x)=⟨eI,x⟩Y_{I}(x)=\left\langle e_{I},x\right\rangle define the drift and carre-du-champ constants by

𝒜Nℓ​YJ=∑|I|≤NbJI​(ℓ)​YI,\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell}Y_{J}=\sum_{|I|\leq N}b^{I}_{J}(\ell)Y_{I},
ΓNℓ​(YJ,YK)\displaystyle\Gamma_{N}^{\ell}(Y_{J},Y_{K}) :=𝒜Nℓ​(YJ​YK)−YJ​𝒜Nℓ​YK−YK​𝒜Nℓ​YJ\displaystyle:=\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell}(Y_{J}Y_{K})-Y_{J}\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell}Y_{K}-Y_{K}\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell}Y_{J}
=∑|I|≤NΓJ,KI​(ℓ)​YI.\displaystyle=\sum_{|I|\leq N}\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell)Y_{I}.

The finite Riccati vector field is

ℛN​(u)I=∑|J|≤NbJI​(ℓ)​uJ+12​∑|J|,|K|≤NΓJ,KI​(ℓ)​uJ​uK,|I|≤N.\mathcal{R}_{N}(u)_{I}=\sum_{|J|\leq N}b^{I}_{J}(\ell)u_{J}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{|J|,|K|\leq N}\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell)u_{J}u_{K},\qquad|I|\leq N.

The infinite-dimensional Riccati operator ℛ\mathcal{R} on TwT_{w} is the projective weighted limit of the compatible family (ℛN)N(\mathcal{R}_{N})_{N} on the finitely supported core 𝒟fin\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fin}}, extended to its local domain by the Lipschitz estimate of Lemma 2.20. Equivalently, ℛ\mathcal{R} is the unique vector field for which

𝒜Nℓ​exp⁡{⟨u,x⟩}=⟨ℛN​(u),x⟩​exp⁡{⟨u,x⟩}\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell}\exp\{\left\langle u,x\right\rangle\}=\left\langle\mathcal{R}_{N}(u),x\right\rangle\exp\{\left\langle u,x\right\rangle\}

for every finitely supported uu inside the finite transform domain. This definition uses the structural constants of the shuffle Hopf algebra through the carre-du-champ. It does not mean that a coefficient depending only on the output word II may be inserted inside an unrestricted sum over all shuffle pairs (J,K)(J,K).

Remark 2.19 (Black–Scholes normalisation check).

In the pure prolonged-signature state the empty-word coordinate is constant and its generator component is zero. The scalar Black–Scholes Riccati equation appears only after adjoining the log-price coordinate Xt=log⁡StX_{t}=\log S_{t} to the state. For

d​Xt=−12​σ2​d​t+σ​d​Bt,dX_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}dt+\sigma dB_{t},

the exponential transform 𝔼⁡[eu​XT∣ℱt]=exp⁡{u​Xt+ϕ⁡(T−t,u)}\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{T}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\exp\{uX_{t}+\phi(T-t,u)\} satisfies

∂τϕ⁡(τ,u)=12​σ2​(u2−u).\partial_{\tau}\phi(\tau,u)=\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}(u^{2}-u).

Thus the normalising Black–Scholes test for the price-extended generator is the coefficient pair (12​σ2,−12​σ2)(\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2},-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}) in the transform variable uu, while the empty word of the pure signature remains constant. This convention is the one used in the generator/carre-du-champ definition of ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Lemma 2.20 (Local Lipschitz property).

The operator ℛ\mathcal{R} is locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of TwT_{w}.

Proof.

The proof is given in Appendix B. It uses the shuffle identity and the Banach algebra estimate for TwT_{w}. ∎

Theorem 2.21 (Local existence of the Riccati flow).

For u0∈Twu_{0}\in T_{w} there exists τ>0\tau>0 such that ∂tut=ℛ⁡(ut)\partial_{t}u_{t}=\mathcal{R}(u_{t}), u0u_{0} given, has a unique classical solution on [0,τ][0,\tau].

Proof.

This is the local Picard–Lindelöf theorem applied to the locally Lipschitz vector field ℛ\mathcal{R}, in the form used for signature SDEs by Cuchiero et al. (2023). ∎

2.6 Truncation, approximation, and measurable recovery

For N≥0N\geq 0 let π≤N:Tw→Tw\pi_{\leq N}:T_{w}\to T_{w} denote the canonical projection onto tensor levels of length at most NN, and set π>N=I−π≤N\pi_{>N}=I-\pi_{\leq N}. Since TwT_{w} is the weighted ℓ1\ell^{1} sum of its homogeneous tensor levels, π≤N​a→a\pi_{\leq N}a\to a in TwT_{w} for every a∈Twa\in T_{w}. The same projections are used in three distinct places: in Section 3 to approximate the volatility functional ⟨ℓ,W^t⟩\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle by finite-level functionals, in Section 5 to define the price-filtration completeness depth, and in Section 6 to express the residual as a limit of finite Gram projections. The notation therefore carries analytic and financial content at the same time.

The following elementary lemma is used repeatedly to pass from finite tensor coordinates to the weighted completion.

Lemma 2.22 (Compatibility of truncation and duality).

Let a∈Twa\in T_{w} and let ℓ∈Tw∗\ell\in T_{w}^{\ast}. Then

⟨ℓ,a⟩=limN→∞⟨π≤N​ℓ,π≤N​a⟩,\left\langle\ell,a\right\rangle=\lim_{N\to\infty}\left\langle\pi_{\leq N}\ell,\pi_{\leq N}a\right\rangle,

and the convergence is absolute. If, in addition, ℓ\ell satisfies H1, then

|⟨ℓ−π≤N​ℓ,a⟩|≤(∑n>Nw⁡(n)​|ℓn|2)1/2​(∑n>Nw​(n)−1​|an|2)1/2.\left\lvert\left\langle\ell-\pi_{\leq N}\ell,a\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\Bigl(\sum_{n>N}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{n>N}w(n)^{-1}\left\lvert a_{n}\right\rvert^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}.
Proof.

The first assertion is the definition of the dual pairing on a weighted direct sum, together with the continuity of the coordinate projections. The second assertion is Cauchy–Schwarz applied level by level to the tail. The estimate is the one used later in the proof of Proposition 3.11: the tail of ℓ\ell and the tail of the signature must be controlled by compatible weights, not by an unweighted summability convention. ∎

Lemma 2.23 (Finite-coordinate measurability).

For every finite set of multi-indices ℐ\mathcal{I}, the random vector

(⟨eI,W^t⟩)I∈ℐ,0≤t≤T,\bigl(\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\bigr)_{I\in\mathcal{I}},\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,

is progressively measurable with respect to ℱW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}, and its terminal value belongs to Lp​(ℱTW^,ℙ)L^{p}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{P}) for every p<∞p<\infty.

Proof.

Progressive measurability follows from construction of the Stratonovich iterated integrals by limits of adapted Riemann sums. The LpL^{p} bound is a finite-dimensional consequence of Proposition 2.12. No infinite-dimensional measurability issue is involved at this stage; the weighted completion enters only after the finite coordinate estimates have been summed with ww. ∎

Remark 2.24 (Why the price filtration is separated from the signature filtration).

The equality ℱtW^=ℱtW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}=\mathcal{F}^{W}_{t} in Theorem 2.8 is a statement about the prolonged Brownian signature. The price filtration ℱtS\mathcal{F}^{S}_{t} is smaller unless the map from the path of WW to the path of SS is invertible after the volatility parameter is fixed. Sections 5 and 6 are formulated on ℱTS\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T} precisely to avoid claiming full Brownian-filtration completeness. Incomplete models such as rough Bergomi remain incomplete in this sense even though their driving Brownian path is encoded in the full prolonged signature.

2.7 Conventions

All processes are right-continuous with left limits. Constants CC, CpC_{p}, CwC_{w}, and Cp,wC_{p,w} depend only on the indicated parameters and may change from line to line. The notation a≲ba\lesssim b means a≤C​ba\leq Cb, and a≍ba\asymp b means a≲ba\lesssim b and b≲ab\lesssim a. Inequalities in TwT_{w} are componentwise. Probability measures are equivalent, written ∼\sim, on ℱTW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T} unless stated otherwise. All subsequent results are formulated in this notation.

3 Theorem A: existence and uniqueness on weighted tensor algebra

3.1 Statement

Theorem 3.1 (Global existence and uniqueness on weighted tensor algebra).

Let ℓ\ell be a signature parameter and let ww be a weight. Assume:

  1. H1.

    ‖ℓ‖2,w2=∑n≥0w⁡(n)​|ℓn|2<∞\displaystyle\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}^{2}=\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}<\infty.

  2. H2.

    ww is increasing, w⁡(0)=1w(0)=1, w⁡(m+n)≤Cw​w​(m)​w​(n)w(m+n)\leq C_{w}w(m)w(n) for some Cw≥1C_{w}\geq 1, and w⁡(n)≤rnw(n)\leq r^{n} for some r>0r>0.

  3. H3.

    With ξt:=⟨ℓ,W^t⟩\xi_{t}:=\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle, the quadratic variation satisfies

    𝔼​exp⁡(λ​∫0Tξs2​𝑑s)​<∞for every ​λ>​0.\mathbb{E}\exp\left(\lambda\int_{0}^{T}\xi_{s}^{2}\,ds\right)<\infty\qquad\text{for every }\lambda>0.

Let s0>0s_{0}>0 be fixed. Then the signature stochastic differential equation

d​St=St​⟨ℓ,W^t⟩​d​Bt,S0=s0,dS_{t}=S_{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\,dB_{t},\qquad S_{0}=s_{0},

admits a unique strong solution S∈C⁡([0,T],(0,∞))S\in C([0,T],(0,\infty)) adapted to ℱW\mathcal{F}^{W}, and

𝔼​supt≤TSt2<∞.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}S_{t}^{2}<\infty.

The solution is strictly positive almost surely. Furthermore, H1 is sharp for the weighted-norm estimates of Section 3.3: Proposition 3.11 exhibits a one-dimensional parameter ℓ\ell and a weight w~\widetilde{w} satisfying H2 but with ∑nw~​(n)​|ℓn|2=+∞\sum_{n}\widetilde{w}(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}=+\infty, for which the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz control of ∫0T⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds used in the existence proof becomes unavailable.

3.2 Strategy of proof

The proof uses the linear structure of the signature SDE. Section 3.3 proves that the volatility process ξt=⟨ℓ,W^t⟩\xi_{t}=\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle is square-integrable on [0,T][0,T]. Section 3.4 constructs the solution as the stochastic exponential s0​ℰ​(M)s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M) of the martingale Mt=∫0tξs​d​BsM_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\xi_{s}\,dB_{s}. Section 3.5 proves uniqueness by localisation. Section 3.7 records the precise admissible-weight class used by the estimates.

3.3 Moment bounds

Lemma 3.2 (Signature moment for pairings).

Assume H1 and H2. For every p∈[1,∞)p\in[1,\infty) and every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T],

𝔼​|⟨ℓ,W^t⟩|p≤Cp,w,T​‖ℓ‖2,wp.\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{p}\leq C_{p,w,T}\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}^{p}.
Proof.

Cauchy–Schwarz in the weighted tensor levels gives

|⟨ℓ,W^t⟩|≤‖ℓ‖2,w​‖W^t‖2,w−1.\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}\left\lVert\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{2,w^{-1}}.

Since ww is increasing and w⁡(0)=1w(0)=1, one has w​(n)−1≤1w(n)^{-1}\leq 1 for all nn. Hence ‖a‖2,w−1≤∑n≥0|an|=‖a‖w0\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{2,w^{-1}}\leq\sum_{n\geq 0}\left\lvert a_{n}\right\rvert=\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w_{0}} for the constant weight w0​(n)=1w_{0}(n)=1, which satisfies the growth bound of Proposition 2.12 with r=1r=1. Proposition 2.12, applied to w0w_{0} with r=1r=1, gives supt≤T𝔼​‖W^t‖2,w−1p<∞\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{2,w^{-1}}^{p}<\infty; the factorial decay of the Brownian iterated integrals dominates the boundary growth rate r=1r=1. The displayed estimate follows. ∎

Lemma 3.3 (Quadratic-variation integrability).

Under H1 and H2,

𝔼​∫0T⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s<∞.\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds<\infty.

Consequently Mt:=∫0t⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​BsM_{t}:=\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s} is a continuous square-integrable martingale.

Proof.

Lemma 3.2 with p=2p=2 and Fubini’s theorem give

𝔼​∫0T⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s=∫0T𝔼​|⟨ℓ,W^s⟩|2​𝑑s≤T​C2,w,T​‖ℓ‖2,w2<∞.\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds=\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\,ds\leq TC_{2,w,T}\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}^{2}<\infty.

The stochastic integral defining MM is therefore well defined and square-integrable on [0,T][0,T]. ∎

Lemma 3.4 (Burkholder–Davis–Gundy estimate with signature integrand).

Let φ\varphi be predictable and satisfy 𝔼​∫0Tφs2​𝑑s<∞\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\varphi_{s}^{2}\,ds<\infty. For every p≥2p\geq 2,

𝔼​supt≤T|∫0tφs​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​Bs|p≤Cp​𝔼​(∫0Tφs2​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s)p/2.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left|\int_{0}^{t}\varphi_{s}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s}\right|^{p}\leq C_{p}\,\mathbb{E}\left(\int_{0}^{T}\varphi_{s}^{2}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds\right)^{p/2}.

Moreover,

𝔼​supt≤T|∫0tφs​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​Bs|p≤Cp,T​𝔼​∫0T|φs|p​|⟨ℓ,W^s⟩|p​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left|\int_{0}^{t}\varphi_{s}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s}\right|^{p}\leq C_{p,T}\,\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\lvert\varphi_{s}\right\rvert^{p}\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{p}\,ds.
Proof.

The first inequality is exactly the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality applied to the stochastic integral. The second follows from Hölder’s inequality in time,

(∫0Tfs2​𝑑s)p/2≤Tp/2−1​∫0Tfsp​𝑑s,\left(\int_{0}^{T}f_{s}^{2}\,ds\right)^{p/2}\leq T^{p/2-1}\int_{0}^{T}f_{s}^{p}\,ds,

with fs=|φs|​|⟨ℓ,W^s⟩|f_{s}=\left\lvert\varphi_{s}\right\rvert\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\right\rvert. ∎

3.4 Construction by stochastic exponential

Proposition 3.5 (Existence).

Under H1–H3, the process

St=s0​ℰ​(M)t=s0​exp⁡(∫0t⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​Bs−12​∫0t⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s)S_{t}=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}=s_{0}\exp\left(\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds\right)

is a strong solution of the signature SDE on [0,T][0,T].

Proof.

Lemma 3.3 makes MM a continuous square-integrable martingale. The Doléans–Dade exponential ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) is therefore a well-defined continuous positive local martingale. Itô’s formula for stochastic exponentials gives

d​ℰ​(M)t=ℰ​(M)t​d​Mt=ℰ​(M)t​⟨ℓ,W^t⟩​d​Bt.d\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}=\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}\,dM_{t}=\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\,dB_{t}.

Multiplying by s0s_{0} yields d​St=St​⟨ℓ,W^t⟩​d​BtdS_{t}=S_{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\,dB_{t} and S0=s0S_{0}=s_{0}. ∎

Proposition 3.6 (Square-integrability of the solution).

Under H3,

𝔼​supt≤TSt2<∞.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}S_{t}^{2}<\infty.
Proof.

Set VT:=⟨M⟩T=∫0T⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑sV_{T}:=\langle M\rangle_{T}=\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}ds. H3 implies the following exponential-integrability consequence: for every α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and every β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R},

𝔼​exp⁡(α​MT+β​VT)<∞.\mathbb{E}\exp(\alpha M_{T}+\beta V_{T})<\infty.

Indeed, fix p>1p>1 and let p′=p/(p−1)p^{\prime}=p/(p-1). Since

exp⁡(α​MT+β​VT)=ℰ​(p​α​M)T1/p​exp⁡((β+12​p​α2)​VT),\exp(\alpha M_{T}+\beta V_{T})=\mathcal{E}(p\alpha M)_{T}^{1/p}\exp\!\left(\bigl(\beta+\tfrac{1}{2}p\alpha^{2}\bigr)\,V_{T}\right),

Hölder’s inequality gives

𝔼​exp⁡(α​MT+β​VT)≤(𝔼​ℰ​(p​α​M)T)1/p​(𝔼​exp⁡(p′​(β+12​p​α2)​VT))1/p′.\mathbb{E}\exp(\alpha M_{T}+\beta V_{T})\leq\bigl(\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}(p\alpha M)_{T}\bigr)^{1/p}\left(\mathbb{E}\exp\left(p^{\prime}\bigl(\beta+\tfrac{1}{2}p\alpha^{2}\bigr)V_{T}\right)\right)^{1/p^{\prime}}.

The first factor equals one by Novikov’s condition for p​α​Mp\alpha M, which is included in H3. The second factor is finite by H3 whenever the coefficient is positive and is bounded by one when the coefficient is non-positive.

Now put Yt:=ℰ​(M)t2Y_{t}:=\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}^{2}. Itô’s formula gives d​Yt=2​Yt​d​Mt+Yt​d​⟨M⟩tdY_{t}=2Y_{t}\,dM_{t}+Y_{t}\,d\langle M\rangle_{t}, so YY is a positive submartingale. Choose q>1q>1. By Doob’s LqL^{q} inequality,

𝔼​supt≤TYt≤(𝔼​supt≤TYtq)1/q≤qq−1​(𝔼​YTq)1/q.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}Y_{t}\leq\left(\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}Y_{t}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\leq\frac{q}{q-1}\left(\mathbb{E}Y_{T}^{q}\right)^{1/q}.

The preceding exponential-integrability consequence, applied with α=2​q\alpha=2q and β=−q\beta=-q, gives

𝔼​YTq=𝔼​exp⁡(2​q​MT−q​VT)<∞.\mathbb{E}Y_{T}^{q}=\mathbb{E}\exp(2qM_{T}-qV_{T})<\infty.

Therefore 𝔼​supt≤Tℰ​(M)t2<∞\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}^{2}<\infty, and multiplication by s02s_{0}^{2} gives the asserted bound. ∎

3.5 Uniqueness

Proposition 3.7 (Uniqueness).

If S(1)S^{(1)} and S(2)S^{(2)} are two strong solutions with 𝔼​supt≤T|St(i)|2<∞\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lvert S_{t}^{(i)}\right\rvert^{2}<\infty, then S(1)=S(2)S^{(1)}=S^{(2)} almost surely.

Proof.

Let ξt=⟨ℓ,W^t⟩\xi_{t}=\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle and let Δt=St(1)−St(2)\Delta_{t}=S_{t}^{(1)}-S_{t}^{(2)}. Then

Δt=∫0tΔs​ξs​d​Bs.\Delta_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\Delta_{s}\xi_{s}\,dB_{s}.

For m≥1m\geq 1, set τm=inf{t≤T:|ξt|≥m}∧T\tau_{m}=\inf\{t\leq T:\left\lvert\xi_{t}\right\rvert\geq m\}\wedge T. Since ξ\xi is continuous, τm↑T\tau_{m}\uparrow T almost surely. Itô isometry gives

𝔼​|Δt∧τm|2=𝔼​∫0t∧τmΔs2​ξs2​𝑑s≤m2​∫0t𝔼​|Δs∧τm|2​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\Delta_{t\wedge\tau_{m}}\right\rvert^{2}=\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{m}}\Delta_{s}^{2}\xi_{s}^{2}\,ds\leq m^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\Delta_{s\wedge\tau_{m}}\right\rvert^{2}\,ds.

Gronwall’s lemma yields 𝔼​|Δt∧τm|2=0\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\Delta_{t\wedge\tau_{m}}\right\rvert^{2}=0 for every t≤Tt\leq T. Letting m→∞m\to\infty gives Δt=0\Delta_{t}=0 for every t≤Tt\leq T, and continuity gives indistinguishability. ∎

3.6 Strict positivity

Proposition 3.8 (Strict positivity).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, ℙ⁡(St>0​ for all ​t≤T)=1\mathbb{P}(S_{t}>0\text{ for all }t\leq T)=1.

Proof.

Proposition 3.5 gives St=s0​ℰ​(M)tS_{t}=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}. The Doléans–Dade exponential of a continuous martingale is strictly positive on finite time intervals. Since s0>0s_{0}>0, St>0S_{t}>0 for all t≤Tt\leq T almost surely. ∎

3.7 The class of admissible weights

Definition 3.9 (Class of admissible weights).

Given ℓ\ell, the class of ℓ\ell-admissible weights is

𝒲(ℓ):={w:ℕ→(0,∞):w satisfies H2 and ∑n≥0w(n)|ℓn|2<∞}.\mathcal{W}(\ell):=\left\{w:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty):w\text{ satisfies H2 and }\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}<\infty\right\}.
Remark 3.10 (Admissibility, weighted norms, and the role of H3).

The class 𝒲⁡(ℓ)\mathcal{W}(\ell) is intrinsic to the pair (ℓ,w)(\ell,w) in the following operational sense. The estimates in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 use ℓ\ell only through ‖ℓ‖2,w2=∑n≥0w⁡(n)​|ℓn|2\left\lVert\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}^{2}=\sum_{n\geq 0}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2} and use ww only through H2 and the Brownian signature moment bound. H1 is therefore not a separate analytic convention; it is the weighted square-summability condition required to define and bound the signature-volatility martingale Mt=∫0t⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​BsM_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s} in L2​(ℙ)L^{2}(\mathbb{P}). Hypothesis H3 plays a distinct role: it upgrades the positive local stochastic exponential ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) to the square-integrable solution class used in subsequent sections. The combination H1–H3 is the hypothesis triple for the constructions of this paper, and Proposition 3.11 shows that H1 cannot be weakened to a weight outside 𝒲⁡(ℓ)\mathcal{W}(\ell) without losing the weighted-norm control.

Proposition 3.11 (Sharpness of H1).

There exist a one-dimensional parameter ℓ\ell and a weight w~\widetilde{w} satisfying w~​(0)=1\widetilde{w}(0)=1 and H2 such that ∑n≥1w~​(n)​|ℓn|2=∞\sum_{n\geq 1}\widetilde{w}(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}=\infty and the weighted L2L^{2} control of ∫0T⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}ds through Lemma 3.2 fails.

Proof.

Let ℓ0=0\ell_{0}=0, ℓn=n−1/2\ell_{n}=n^{-1/2} for n≥1n\geq 1 and let w~​(n)=n+1\widetilde{w}(n)=n+1. Then w~​(0)=1\widetilde{w}(0)=1 and w~​(m+n)≤w~​(m)​w~​(n)\widetilde{w}(m+n)\leq\widetilde{w}(m)\widetilde{w}(n), so H2 holds. Moreover,

∑n≥1w~​(n)​|ℓn|2=∑n≥1n+1n=∞.\sum_{n\geq 1}\widetilde{w}(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}=\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{n+1}{n}=\infty.

The weighted Cauchy–Schwarz estimate of Lemma 3.2 would bound

𝔼​∫0T|⟨ℓ,W^s⟩|2​𝑑s\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\lvert\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}ds

by a constant multiple of ∑nw~​(n)​|ℓn|2\sum_{n}\widetilde{w}(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}, which is infinite for this choice. Lemma 3.3 is therefore unavailable under w~\widetilde{w}, and the square-integrable martingale property of MM used in Proposition 3.5 cannot be obtained from the weighted tensor estimate. Thus H1 is exactly the summability condition required by the proof. ∎

3.8 Finite-level localisation of the exponential construction

For N≥0N\geq 0 define the truncated volatility functional

ξtN:=⟨π≤N​ℓ,W^t⟩,MtN:=∫0tξsN​d​Bs,StN:=s0​ℰ​(MN)t.\xi^{N}_{t}:=\left\langle\pi_{\leq N}\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle,\qquad M^{N}_{t}:=\int_{0}^{t}\xi^{N}_{s}\,dB_{s},\qquad S^{N}_{t}:=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M^{N})_{t}.

The process SNS^{N} is the finite-coordinate signature-volatility approximation of the solution. It is useful because every coefficient in ξN\xi^{N} is a finite linear combination of iterated Stratonovich integrals, so all stochastic calculus operations may first be performed at finite level and then passed to the limit. The next lemma records the convergence statement needed for this passage.

Lemma 3.12 (Convergence of finite-level stochastic exponentials).

Assume H1–H3. Then

𝔼​∫0T|ξsN−ξs|2​𝑑s→0,𝔼​supt≤T|MtN−Mt|2→0.\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\lvert\xi^{N}_{s}-\xi_{s}\right\rvert^{2}\,ds\to 0,\qquad\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lvert M^{N}_{t}-M_{t}\right\rvert^{2}\to 0.

Moreover, for every q∈(1,2)q\in(1,2) for which the exponential moment supplied by H3 is finite with the required constant,

SN→SinLq​(Ω,C⁡([0,T])).S^{N}\to S\quad\hbox{in}\quad L^{q}\bigl(\Omega;C([0,T])\bigr).
Proof.

By Lemma 2.22,

|ξsN−ξs|2≤(∑n>Nw⁡(n)​|ℓn|2)​(∑n>Nw​(n)−1​|(W^s)n|2).\left\lvert\xi^{N}_{s}-\xi_{s}\right\rvert^{2}\leq\Bigl(\sum_{n>N}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{n>N}w(n)^{-1}\left\lvert(\widehat{W}_{s})_{n}\right\rvert^{2}\Bigr).

The first factor tends to zero by H1, while the second factor is dominated in L1​(d​s⊗d​ℙ)L^{1}(ds\otimes d\mathbb{P}) by the Brownian signature moment bound. Dominated convergence gives the first limit. The second limit follows from Itô isometry and the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality. For the stochastic exponentials, write

ℰ​(MN)t−ℰ​(M)t=ℰ​(M)t​(exp⁡{(MtN−Mt)−12​(⟨MN⟩t−⟨M⟩t)}−1),\mathcal{E}(M^{N})_{t}-\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}=\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}\left(\exp\{(M^{N}_{t}-M_{t})-\tfrac{1}{2}(\langle M^{N}\rangle_{t}-\langle M\rangle_{t})\}-1\right),

localise by supt(|Mt|+|MtN|+⟨M⟩t+⟨MN⟩t)≤R\sup_{t}(\left\lvert M_{t}\right\rvert+\left\lvert M^{N}_{t}\right\rvert+\langle M\rangle_{t}+\langle M^{N}\rangle_{t})\leq R, pass to the limit on the localised set, and then let R→∞R\to\infty using the exponential-integrability consequence of H3. This gives convergence in the asserted range of qq. ∎

Proposition 3.13 (Stability with respect to the signature parameter).

Let ℓ(m)→ℓ\ell^{(m)}\to\ell in the weighted Hilbert norm ‖⋅‖2,w\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2,w}, and assume that H3 holds uniformly for the corresponding volatility functionals ξ(m)\xi^{(m)} in the sense that

supm𝔼​exp⁡(λ​∫0T|ξs(m)|2​𝑑s)​<∞for every ​λ>​0.\sup_{m}\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl(\lambda\int_{0}^{T}\left\lvert\xi^{(m)}_{s}\right\rvert^{2}\,ds\Bigr)<\infty\quad\hbox{for every }\lambda>0.

Let S(m)S^{(m)} be the solution associated with ℓ(m)\ell^{(m)}. Then S(m)→SS^{(m)}\to S in Lq​(Ω,C⁡([0,T]))L^{q}(\Omega;C([0,T])) for every q<2q<2.

Proof.

The proof is identical to the finite-level argument, with ℓ(m)−ℓ\ell^{(m)}-\ell replacing the tail ℓ−π≤N​ℓ\ell-\pi_{\leq N}\ell. The uniform H3 bound gives uniform integrability of the stochastic exponentials and prevents the local convergence of martingales from degenerating at the exponential step. Thus the solution map is continuous on every subset of the parameter space on which H3 is uniform. ∎

Remark 3.14 (Role of H3 in the square-integrable class).

The construction of S=s0​ℰ​(M)S=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M) requires only local square integrability of MM for local existence and positivity. The paper needs the stronger conclusion 𝔼​supt≤TSt2<∞\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}S_{t}^{2}<\infty because Sections 4–6 operate in L2L^{2} spaces. Hypothesis H3 is exactly the bridge between those two levels: it converts the stochastic exponential from a positive local martingale into a true object in the Hilbert space used for asset pricing and hedging.

3.9 Closed estimates used later

The preceding proof yields three estimates that are used implicitly in the FTAP and hedging sections. First, for every p≥2p\geq 2 there is a finite constant Cp,T,w,ℓC_{p,T,w,\ell} such that

𝔼​supt≤T|Mt|p≤Cp,T,w,ℓ.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lvert M_{t}\right\rvert^{p}\leq C_{p,T,w,\ell}.

Second, for every admissible strategy HH,

𝔼ℚ​(∫0THs2​Ss2​ξs2​𝑑s)<∞\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left(\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}^{2}S_{s}^{2}\xi_{s}^{2}\,ds\right)<\infty

whenever the Radon–Nikodym density d​ℚ/d​ℙd\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P} has an LrL^{r} moment for some r>1r>1 compatible with H3. Third, finite-level approximations commute with the GKW projection: if XX is approximated by a polynomial in finitely many terminal signature coordinates, then the stochastic-integral component of its projection is the limit of the projections of the finite approximants. This last property follows from closedness of the stochastic-integral subspace in L2L^{2} and is the analytic link between Theorem A and Theorem D.

3.10 Uniform integrability and localisation

The square-integrability proof in Proposition 3.6 may be rewritten as a two-layer localisation argument. Let

τR:=inf{t≤T:⟨M⟩t≥R}∧T.\tau_{R}:=\inf\{t\leq T:\langle M\rangle_{t}\geq R\}\wedge T.

On [0,τR][0,\tau_{R}], the stochastic exponential ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) has moments of every order by Novikov with a deterministic bound depending on RR. Therefore

𝔼​supt≤Tℰ​(M)t∧τR2<∞.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\mathcal{E}(M)_{t\wedge\tau_{R}}^{2}<\infty.

The passage R→∞R\to\infty is justified by H3. Indeed,

ℙ⁡(τR<T)=ℙ⁡(⟨M⟩T>R)≤e−λ​R​𝔼​eλ​⟨M⟩T,\mathbb{P}(\tau_{R}<T)=\mathbb{P}(\langle M\rangle_{T}>R)\leq e^{-\lambda R}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\langle M\rangle_{T}},

and the right-hand side tends to zero for every fixed λ>0\lambda>0. The exponential moment also gives uniform integrability of the stopped supremum, so the stopped estimates converge to the unstopped estimate.

This localisation is used in Section 4 under equivalent measures. If ZT=d​ℚ/d​ℙZ_{T}=d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P} satisfies ZT∈Lr​(ℙ)Z_{T}\in L^{r}(\mathbb{P}) for some r>1r>1, then Hölder gives

𝔼ℚ​supt≤TSt2≤‖ZT‖Lr​(ℙ)​(𝔼ℙ​(supt≤TSt2)r/(r−1))(r−1)/r.\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\sup_{t\leq T}S_{t}^{2}\leq\left\lVert Z_{T}\right\rVert_{L^{r}(\mathbb{P})}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\sup_{t\leq T}S_{t}^{2}\right)^{r/(r-1)}\right)^{(r-1)/r}.

H3 supplies the higher moment on the right after replacing the exponent in Proposition 3.6 by the corresponding value. Thus the L2L^{2} solution class is stable under the separating measures used in the asset-pricing theorem, as long as the density lies in a compatible LrL^{r} class.

Lemma 3.15 (Localisation of uniqueness).

Let S(1)S^{(1)} and S(2)S^{(2)} be two positive continuous solutions of the signature SDE driven by the same Brownian motion and the same initial value. If ∫0Tξs2​𝑑s<∞\int_{0}^{T}\xi_{s}^{2}ds<\infty almost surely, then the two solutions are indistinguishable without imposing the global L2L^{2} supremum bound.

Proof.

Set Δ=S(1)−S(2)\Delta=S^{(1)}-S^{(2)} and τm=inf{t:|ξt|≥m}∧T\tau_{m}=\inf\{t:\left\lvert\xi_{t}\right\rvert\geq m\}\wedge T. On [0,τm][0,\tau_{m}],

Δt∧τm=∫0t∧τmΔs​ξs​d​Bs.\Delta_{t\wedge\tau_{m}}=\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{m}}\Delta_{s}\xi_{s}\,dB_{s}.

The stopped integrand is bounded by m​|Δs|m\left\lvert\Delta_{s}\right\rvert, and the stopped solutions are continuous on a compact interval. Applying Itô isometry after the additional stopping time ρk=inf{t:|St(1)|+|St(2)|≥k}∧T\rho_{k}=\inf\{t:\left\lvert S^{(1)}_{t}\right\rvert+\left\lvert S^{(2)}_{t}\right\rvert\geq k\}\wedge T gives

𝔼​|Δt∧τm∧ρk|2≤m2​∫0t𝔼​|Δs∧τm∧ρk|2​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\Delta_{t\wedge\tau_{m}\wedge\rho_{k}}\right\rvert^{2}\leq m^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\lvert\Delta_{s\wedge\tau_{m}\wedge\rho_{k}}\right\rvert^{2}ds.

Gronwall gives equality to zero. Letting k→∞k\to\infty and then m→∞m\to\infty proves indistinguishability. ∎

3.11 Truncation-stable form of the existence proof

For N≥0N\geq 0 write πN​ℓ\pi_{N}\ell for the truncation of ℓ\ell to levels at most NN and set

ξt(N):=⟨πN​ℓ,W^t⟩,Mt(N):=∫0tξs(N)​d​Bs,St(N):=s0​ℰ​(M(N))t.\xi_{t}^{(N)}:=\left\langle\pi_{N}\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle,\qquad M_{t}^{(N)}:=\int_{0}^{t}\xi_{s}^{(N)}\,dB_{s},\qquad S_{t}^{(N)}:=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M^{(N)})_{t}.

The finite-level equations are ordinary Itô equations with polynomial coefficients in the Brownian signature. They therefore give a canonical approximating sequence for the infinite equation. The point of the weighted proof is that the estimates do not depend on the dimension of the truncated tensor algebra. Indeed,

𝔼​∫0T|ξs(N)−ξs(M)|2​𝑑s≤CT,w​∑n=M+1Nw⁡(n)​|ℓn|2,N>M,\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\lvert\xi_{s}^{(N)}-\xi_{s}^{(M)}\right\rvert^{2}\,ds\leq C_{T,w}\sum_{n=M+1}^{N}w(n)\left\lvert\ell_{n}\right\rvert^{2},\qquad N>M,

where CT,wC_{T,w} is the moment constant from Proposition 2.12. Hence (M(N))N(M^{(N)})_{N} is Cauchy in L2​(Ω,C​[0,T])L^{2}(\Omega;C[0,T]) after the BDG estimate. The limit is precisely MM because the pairings converge in L2​([0,T]×Ω)L^{2}([0,T]\times\Omega).

The stochastic exponentials also converge. Fix q>1q>1. By H3 and the proof of Proposition 3.6,

supN𝔼​supt≤T|ℰ​(M(N))t|2​q<∞.\sup_{N}\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lvert\mathcal{E}(M^{(N)})_{t}\right\rvert^{2q}<\infty.

The elementary estimate

|ℰ⁡(x)−ℰ⁡(y)|≤exp⁡{|x|+|y|+12​|⟨x⟩|+12​|⟨y⟩|}​(|x−y|+|⟨x⟩−⟨y⟩|)\left\lvert\mathcal{E}(x)-\mathcal{E}(y)\right\rvert\leq\exp\{\left\lvert x\right\rvert+\left\lvert y\right\rvert+\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lvert\langle x\rangle\right\rvert+\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lvert\langle y\rangle\right\rvert\}\bigl(\left\lvert x-y\right\rvert+\left\lvert\langle x\rangle-\langle y\rangle\right\rvert\bigr)

applied to continuous martingales, followed by Hölder and BDG, gives

limN→∞𝔼​supt≤T|St(N)−St|2=0.\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lvert S_{t}^{(N)}-S_{t}\right\rvert^{2}=0.

Thus Theorem 3.1 may be read as a limit theorem for finite signature-volatility SDEs. This is the form needed in Sections 4–6, where the Riccati transform and the Gram systems are first written at finite level and then passed to the weighted limit.

Lemma 3.16 (Stability of the signature-volatility map).

Let ℓ(m)→ℓ\ell^{(m)}\to\ell in the Hilbert norm ‖⋅‖2,w\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2,w} and suppose that H3 holds uniformly for the corresponding pairings in the sense that

supm𝔼​exp⁡(λ​∫0T⟨ℓ(m),W^s⟩2​𝑑s)​<∞for every ​λ>​0.\sup_{m}\mathbb{E}\exp\left(\lambda\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\ell^{(m)},\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}\,ds\right)<\infty\qquad\text{for every }\lambda>0.

Then the associated solutions S(m)S^{(m)} converge to SS in L2​(Ω,C​[0,T])L^{2}(\Omega;C[0,T]).

Proof.

The weighted Cauchy–Schwarz estimate gives

𝔼​∫0T|⟨ℓ(m)−ℓ,W^s⟩|2​𝑑s≤CT,w​‖ℓ(m)−ℓ‖2,w2.\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left\lvert\left\langle\ell^{(m)}-\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\,ds\leq C_{T,w}\left\lVert\ell^{(m)}-\ell\right\rVert_{2,w}^{2}.

BDG gives convergence of the driving martingales in L2​(C​[0,T])L^{2}(C[0,T]). Uniform H3 supplies a common exponential moment for the stochastic-exponential comparison. The displayed estimate for the exponential map then yields convergence of the solutions. No pathwise compactness argument is used; all compactness is carried by the weighted Hilbert norm of the parameter. ∎

Remark 3.17 (Why the proof is not a Picard proof).

The equation for SS is linear once the signature path has been fixed. The stochastic-exponential proof uses this structure directly. A Picard iteration would prove the same existence statement by repeatedly integrating the same multiplicative coefficient, but it would obscure the true-martingale estimate, which is the object needed in the FTAP. The present proof therefore chooses the route that gives the positivity, localisation, and square-integrability statements in one chain.

3.12 Parameter classes and examples of H3

The condition H3 is strong, but it is verifiable in the main examples. If ⟨ℓ,W^t⟩\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle is bounded, H3 is immediate. This covers bounded finite-signature examples, including the sine-signature parameter discussed in Section 4. If ⟨ℓ,W^t⟩\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle is a polynomial of a finite-dimensional Gaussian Markov process, Fernique-type estimates and finite-horizon Gaussian moment bounds give H3 for sufficiently small polynomial growth, and for bounded horizons in the finite-support cases used in Section 7. If the functional is induced by an affine square-root process, H3 is equivalent to the classical finite exponential moment condition for the integrated variance.

The theorem is deliberately stated with H3 rather than with a list of model-specific sufficient conditions. This keeps Theorem 3.1 structural: the existence proof uses only the exponential moment of the quadratic variation, not the mechanism by which that moment is obtained. In applications, H3 is checked by the moment-explosion theory of the chosen model, while H1 and H2 are checked by the tensor coefficients of the signature parameter.

3.13 A final verification of the stochastic-exponential estimates

For later reference we record the exact implication from H3 to the two uniform estimates used in the paper. Let VT=⟨M⟩TV_{T}=\langle M\rangle_{T}. H3 gives 𝔼​exp⁡(λ​VT)<∞\mathbb{E}\exp(\lambda V_{T})<\infty for every λ>0\lambda>0. For a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} write

exp⁡(a​MT+b​VT)=ℰ​(p​a​M)T1/p​exp⁡{(b+12​p​a2)​VT}\exp(aM_{T}+bV_{T})=\mathcal{E}(paM)_{T}^{1/p}\exp\{(b+\tfrac{1}{2}pa^{2})V_{T}\}

for p>1p>1. Hölder’s inequality and Novikov give

𝔼​exp⁡(a​MT+b​VT)≤(𝔼​ℰ​(p​a​M)T)1/p​(𝔼​exp⁡{p′​(b+12​p​a2)​VT})1/p′<∞.\mathbb{E}\exp(aM_{T}+bV_{T})\leq\left(\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}(paM)_{T}\right)^{1/p}\left(\mathbb{E}\exp\{p^{\prime}(b+\tfrac{1}{2}pa^{2})V_{T}\}\right)^{1/p^{\prime}}<\infty.

This proves all exponential moments of the pair (MT,VT)(M_{T},V_{T}) that are used to control suptSt2\sup_{t}S_{t}^{2} and to transport coordinate estimates under equivalent changes of measure.

The same estimate applies to stopped martingales MτM^{\tau} with constants independent of the stopping time. Thus all localisation steps in Sections 3 and 4 are compatible with passage to the limit. This matters because local martingale arguments are first proved for stopped processes, while the theorem statements are global on [0,T][0,T].

Lemma 3.18 (Uniform stopped exponential estimate).

Under H3, for every q>1q>1,

supτ≤T𝔼​supt≤Tℰ​(Mτ)t2​q<∞,\sup_{\tau\leq T}\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\mathcal{E}(M^{\tau})_{t}^{2q}<\infty,

where the supremum is over all stopping times bounded by TT.

Proof.

Doob’s inequality reduces the estimate to the terminal moment of ℰ​(Mτ)T2​q\mathcal{E}(M^{\tau})_{T}^{2q}. The preceding exponential-moment calculation applies with MTM_{T} replaced by MT∧τM_{T\wedge\tau} and VTV_{T} replaced by VT∧τ≤VTV_{T\wedge\tau}\leq V_{T}. H3 controls the resulting exponential moment uniformly in τ\tau. ∎

3.14 Discussion

The local existence result of Cuchiero et al. (2023) operates on the extended tensor algebra for characteristics represented as linear maps of the signature, under integrability hypotheses suited to affine and polynomial transforms. Theorem 3.1 obtains a global existence statement in the weighted Banach algebra TwT_{w} under H1–H3, replacing a pathwise boundedness requirement by weighted square summability of the signature parameter and exponential integrability of the quadratic variation. The two formulations are complementary: the extended-algebra setting is adapted to transform formulae, while the weighted-algebra setting is adapted to moment bounds and to the FTAP statement of Section 4.

H3 is not a cosmetic assumption: it is the condition that upgrades the positive local stochastic exponential ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) to the square-integrable solution class used in the asset-pricing and hedging sections. In the constant-coefficient case ℓ=σ​e∅\ell=\sigma e_{\emptyset}, H3 reduces to ∫0Tσ2​𝑑s<∞\int_{0}^{T}\sigma^{2}ds<\infty, which is immediate. In the rough-Bergomi example of Section 7.4, H3 follows from Gaussian exponential-moment estimates on finite horizons after truncation and localisation. The pathwise existence problem under weaker, non-exponential integrability assumptions is left open.

4 Theorem B: asset pricing and transform non-explosion

4.1 Statement

Lemma 4.1 (Special-semimartingale property of signature coordinates).

Assume H1, H2, and H3. Let ℚ∼ℙ\mathbb{Q}\sim\mathbb{P} on ℱTW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T} with bounded density d​ℚ/d​ℙ∈L∞​(ℙ)d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{P}). For every multi-index II with |I|≥1|I|\geq 1, the process (⟨eI,W^t⟩)0≤t≤T(\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle)_{0\leq t\leq T} is a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-special semimartingale whose canonical decomposition

⟨eI,W^t⟩=⟨eI,W^0⟩+MtI+AtI\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle=\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{0}\right\rangle+M_{t}^{I}+A_{t}^{I}

has continuous local-martingale part MIM^{I} and continuous predictable finite-variation part AIA^{I}. Furthermore, MIM^{I} is a true ℚ\mathbb{Q}-martingale on [0,T][0,T] and AIA^{I} has integrable variation.

Proof.

The coordinate ⟨eI,W^t⟩\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle is an iterated Stratonovich integral of the time-augmented Brownian path. Proposition 2.12, applied to the finite set of levels up to |I||I|, gives

supt≤T𝔼ℙ​|⟨eI,W^t⟩|2<∞.\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\left\lvert\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}<\infty.

The Stratonovich-to-Itô conversion formula writes this iterated Stratonovich integral as a finite sum of Itô iterated integrals plus bracket terms. The Itô iterated integrals are continuous local martingales. The bracket terms are continuous predictable processes of finite variation, since each contraction in the conversion replaces two Brownian differentials by a Lebesgue-time differential and leaves at most |I|−2|I|-2 stochastic integrations.

The density bound transports the estimate from ℙ\mathbb{P} to ℚ\mathbb{Q}:

supt≤T𝔼ℚ​|⟨eI,W^t⟩|2≤‖d​ℚ/d​ℙ‖L∞​(ℙ)​supt≤T𝔼ℙ​|⟨eI,W^t⟩|2<∞.\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left\lvert\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\leq\left\lVert d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P}\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{P})}\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\left\lvert\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}<\infty.

Hence every local-martingale component produced by the conversion is square-integrable under ℚ\mathbb{Q} and is therefore a true martingale. The same bound, applied to the finitely many bracket terms, gives integrable variation of AIA^{I}. This is the canonical special-semimartingale decomposition, because continuous local martingales and continuous predictable finite-variation processes have unique decomposition. ∎

Theorem 4.2 (Signature asset-pricing and transform theorem).

Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1. Then the following assertions hold.

  1. (i)

    The model satisfies NFLVR on the signature filtration ℱtW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t} in the Delbaen–Schachermayer sense adapted to predictable signature-integrable strategies. More precisely, ℙ\mathbb{P} itself is an equivalent true-martingale measure for SS, and every finite signature coordinate ⟨eI,W^t⟩\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle is a ℙ\mathbb{P}-special semimartingale whose canonical martingale part is a true martingale.

  2. (ii)

    Let ℚ∼ℙ\mathbb{Q}\sim\mathbb{P} be an equivalent measure under which SS is a true ℚ\mathbb{Q}-martingale and the finite signature-coordinate transforms are finite on [0,T][0,T] for all initial data in 𝒟fin\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fin}}. Then, under the standing hypotheses H1–H3 (which supply the finite-coordinate moment and uniform-integrability bounds used in the identification step), the conditional transform is exponential-affine on each finite truncation if and only if the Riccati equation ∂tut=ℛ⁡(ut)\partial_{t}u_{t}=\mathcal{R}(u_{t}) admits a global solution on [0,T][0,T] for every such finitely supported initial condition.

Consequently, global Riccati solvability is a transform non-explosion condition. It is not asserted to be equivalent to NFLVR under H1–H3 alone.

4.2 NFLVR on the signature filtration

Definition 4.3 (NFLVR).

The signature SDE satisfies No Free Lunch with Vanishing Risk on ℱW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}} in the sense of Delbaen and Schachermayer (1994) if the cone

𝒞:={VTH−f:H is admissible in the sense of Definition 2.17,f≥0}∩L∞(ℱTW^,ℙ)\mathcal{C}:=\{V_{T}^{H}-f:H\text{ is admissible in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:admissible-strategies}},\ f\geq 0\}\cap L^{\infty}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{P})

satisfies

𝒞¯σ⁡(L∞,L1)∩L+∞​(ℱTW^,ℙ)={0}.\overline{\mathcal{C}}^{\sigma(L^{\infty},L^{1})}\cap L_{+}^{\infty}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{P})=\{0\}.
Theorem 4.4 (Kreps–Yan separation).

The set of bounded admissible terminal wealths is weak-∗\ast closed in L∞​(ℱTW^,ℙ)L^{\infty}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{P}).

Proof.

The proof is the Kreps–Yan closed-cone argument applied on the recovered Brownian filtration. The equality ℱtW^=ℱtW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}=\mathcal{F}^{W}_{t} in Theorem 2.8 removes the only possible filtration ambiguity: every ℱW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}-predictable integrand has an indistinguishable ℱW\mathcal{F}^{W}-predictable version, and conversely every ℱW\mathcal{F}^{W}-predictable integrand is measurable with respect to the first level of the prolonged signature. The stochastic integral ∫H​𝑑S\int H\,dS is therefore the same object whether it is viewed on the Brownian filtration or on the prolonged-signature filtration.

Closedness follows from the standard semimartingale topology. If HnH^{n} is a sequence of admissible integrands whose terminal wealths are bounded from below and converge weak-∗\ast in L∞L^{\infty}, the Emery-topology closedness theorem for stochastic-integral cones gives a limiting predictable integrand HH after localisation. The admissibility condition in Definition 2.17 is stable under this localisation because the quadratic variation of the stochastic integral is

∫0T|Hs|2​Ss2​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s.\int_{0}^{T}|H_{s}|^{2}S_{s}^{2}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}ds.

Fatou’s lemma preserves finiteness of this quantity. This proves weak-∗\ast closedness of the bounded terminal wealth cone. The separation theorem of Kreps (1981) and Yan (1980), in the Delbaen–Schachermayer formulation, then supplies a strictly positive separating functional whenever NFLVR holds. ∎

Lemma 4.5 (Localisation stability of admissible gains).

Let HH be admissible in the sense of Definition 2.17 and let (τm)(\tau_{m}) be an increasing sequence of stopping times with τm↑T\tau_{m}\uparrow T. Then H​𝟏[0,τm]H\mathbf{1}_{[0,\tau_{m}]} is admissible for every mm, and

∫0τm|Hs|2​Ss2​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s↑∫0T|Hs|2​Ss2​⟨ℓ,W^s⟩2​𝑑s.\int_{0}^{\tau_{m}}|H_{s}|^{2}S_{s}^{2}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}ds\uparrow\int_{0}^{T}|H_{s}|^{2}S_{s}^{2}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle^{2}ds.

If the stopped terminal gains converge in L2​(ℚ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}), their limit is the terminal gain of the original admissible strategy.

Proof.

The first assertion is immediate from monotonicity of the non-negative quadratic-variation density. The stopped stochastic integral is

∫0THs​𝟏[0,τm]​(s)​d​Ss=∫0τmHs​d​Ss.\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\mathbf{1}_{[0,\tau_{m}]}(s)dS_{s}=\int_{0}^{\tau_{m}}H_{s}\,dS_{s}.

It is square-integrable under the equivalent martingale measure whenever the displayed quadratic variation has finite expectation. Monotone convergence gives the increasing limit of the quadratic variations. If the terminal stopped gains converge in L2​(ℚ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}), the Itô isometry identifies the limit with the stochastic integral of HH on [0,T][0,T] after passage to an indistinguishable predictable version. This is the stability used in the closedness argument of Theorem 4.4. ∎

Lemma 4.6 (True-martingale upgrade under H3).

Let Mt=∫0t⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​BsM_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s}. Under H3, ℰ⁡(α​M)\mathcal{E}(\alpha M) is a true martingale for every α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, and ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) is uniformly integrable on [0,T][0,T].

Proof.

Novikov’s condition for α​M\alpha M is

𝔼​exp⁡(12​α2​⟨M⟩T)<∞,\mathbb{E}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\alpha^{2}\langle M\rangle_{T}\right)<\infty,

which is exactly H3 with λ=α2/2\lambda=\alpha^{2}/2. Hence ℰ⁡(α​M)\mathcal{E}(\alpha M) is a true martingale for each fixed α\alpha. Uniform integrability of ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) follows from an explicit higher-moment estimate. For p>1p>1,

ℰ​(M)Tp=ℰ​(p​M)T​exp⁡{12​(p2−p)​⟨M⟩T}.\mathcal{E}(M)_{T}^{p}=\mathcal{E}(pM)_{T}\exp\left\{\frac{1}{2}(p^{2}-p)\langle M\rangle_{T}\right\}.

Choose q>1q>1 and let q′=q/(q−1)q^{\prime}=q/(q-1). Holder’s inequality gives

𝔼​ℰ​(M)Tp≤(𝔼​ℰ​(p​q​M)T)1/q​(𝔼​exp⁡{12​q′​(p2−p)​⟨M⟩T})1/q′<∞,\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}(M)_{T}^{p}\leq\bigl(\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}(pqM)_{T}\bigr)^{1/q}\left(\mathbb{E}\exp\left\{\frac{1}{2}q^{\prime}(p^{2}-p)\langle M\rangle_{T}\right\}\right)^{1/q^{\prime}}<\infty,

where the first factor is one by Novikov for p​q​MpqM and the second is finite by H3. Thus ℰ​(M)T\mathcal{E}(M)_{T} has an LpL^{p} moment for some p>1p>1, which implies uniform integrability of the martingale family. ∎

4.3 Proof of the martingale and NFLVR assertion

Proof of Theorem 4.2(i).

Set

Mt=∫0t⟨ℓ,W^s⟩​d​Bs,St=s0​ℰ​(M)t.M_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle\ell,\widehat{W}_{s}\right\rangle\,dB_{s},\qquad S_{t}=s_{0}\mathcal{E}(M)_{t}.

By H3, Novikov’s condition holds for every scalar multiple of MM. Lemma 4.6 therefore gives that ℰ⁡(M)\mathcal{E}(M) is a uniformly integrable true martingale. Hence SS is a true martingale under the reference measure ℙ\mathbb{P} itself. Thus ℚ:=ℙ\mathbb{Q}:=\mathbb{P} is an equivalent true-martingale measure for SS.

The special-semimartingale statement for the signature coordinates follows from the Stratonovich-to-Itô conversion exactly as in Lemma 4.1, applied in the special case ℚ=ℙ\mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{P} (constant density 11, which lies in L∞​(ℙ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{P})). Each coordinate is a finite iterated Stratonovich integral, hence a finite sum of Itô iterated integrals plus bracket corrections. The martingale terms have finite moments by Proposition 2.12 and are true martingales.

The Delbaen–Schachermayer theorem applied on the recovered Brownian filtration ℱW^=ℱW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}=\mathcal{F}^{W} now yields NFLVR for the admissible wealth cone of Definition 2.17. No Brownian drift shift is needed: the discounted price already has zero drift under the reference measure and is a true martingale by H3. ∎

4.4 Proof of the transform/Riccati assertion

Proof of Theorem 4.2(ii).

Fix a finite truncation NN and a finitely supported transform direction uu. Under the stated transform-finiteness hypothesis, the conditional transform

ΛtN​(u)=𝔼ℚ​[exp⁡{⟨u,W^T(N)⟩}∣ℱtW^]\Lambda_{t}^{N}(u)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left[\exp\{\left\langle u,\widehat{W}_{T}^{(N)}\right\rangle\}\mid\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}\right]

is finite and is a true martingale. The affine-polynomial structure of the prolonged signature gives the finite-dimensional ansatz

ΛtN​(u)=exp⁡{⟨ψN​(T−t,u),W^t(N)⟩}\Lambda_{t}^{N}(u)=\exp\{\left\langle\psi_{N}(T-t,u),\widehat{W}_{t}^{(N)}\right\rangle\}

on the transform domain. Applying Itô’s formula to the right-hand side and equating the drift to zero gives

∂τψN​(τ,u)=ℛN​(ψN​(τ,u)),ψN​(0,u)=u,\partial_{\tau}\psi_{N}(\tau,u)=\mathcal{R}_{N}(\psi_{N}(\tau,u)),\qquad\psi_{N}(0,u)=u,

where ℛN\mathcal{R}_{N} is the generator/carre-du-champ vector field of Definition 2.18. The quadratic coefficients are the structural constants ΓJ,KI​(ℓ)\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell), not an output-only coefficient placed inside an unrestricted shuffle-pair sum.

If the finite Riccati solution exploded before TT, the exponential-affine expression would cease to represent a finite conditional expectation in the corresponding transform direction. This contradicts the assumed finiteness of ΛN​(u)\Lambda^{N}(u) on the whole horizon. Hence transform finiteness implies global Riccati solvability on the finitely supported core.

Conversely, if the Riccati solution is global on [0,T][0,T] and remains in the finite transform domain, the exponential-affine expression is a finite positive local martingale. The finite-coordinate moment estimates and H3 give the uniform-integrability bound needed to identify it with the conditional transform. Passing from finite NN to the weighted core uses Lemma 4.10. This proves the stated equivalence between transform non-explosion and global Riccati solvability. ∎

4.5 Riccati solvability as a separate transform condition

Remark 4.7 (Riccati solvability is a separate transform-domain hypothesis).

Status of the sharpness example. The bounded sine example used in earlier drafts verifies H1–H3 but does not, by itself, prove finite-time blow-up of a Riccati coordinate. The reason is structural: the level-two equation contains a positive contribution proportional to u12u_{1}^{2}, while the lower-level coordinate u1u_{1} need not satisfy a self-quadratic Riccati inequality. Hence the three-coordinate comparison with y˙=a2​y2−C​y−D\dot{y}=a^{2}y^{2}-Cy-D is not a valid proof of explosion and is not used in the theorem chain.

The conclusion retained in this paper is the logically weaker and correct one. H3 implies the true-martingale/NFLVR statement for the price process under the reference measure, whereas global solvability of the Riccati equation is a transform non-explosion condition for finite signature Fourier–Laplace directions. The latter must be imposed or checked separately in applications. In one-dimensional odd-order signature-volatility models, finite-time transform explosion is supplied by the moment-explosion theorem of Abi Jaber et al. (2025); in finite-dimensional polynomial examples it can also be checked directly from the corresponding finite Riccati system. No self-contained blow-up counterexample is claimed here.

4.6 Closedness and separation details

The proof of Theorem 4.2 uses the Delbaen–Schachermayer separation mechanism only after the class of admissible integrands has been fixed. Let

𝒦:={∫0THs​d​Ss:H​ is ​S​-admissible and the stochastic integral is bounded from below}.\mathcal{K}:=\left\{\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\,dS_{s}:H\hbox{ is }S\hbox{-admissible and the stochastic integral is bounded from below}\right\}.

The relevant cone is 𝒞=(𝒦−L+0)∩L∞​(ℱTW^,ℙ)\mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{K}-L^{0}_{+})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{P}). NFLVR is the statement that the weak-star closure of 𝒞\mathcal{C} in L∞L^{\infty} meets L+∞L^{\infty}_{+} only at zero. The signature structure enters in the proof of closedness through the identity ℱtW^=ℱtW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}=\mathcal{F}^{W}_{t}: admissible stochastic integrals are stochastic integrals on a Brownian filtration, but their integrability is measured with the random weight St2​ξt2S_{t}^{2}\xi_{t}^{2} induced by the signature parameter.

Lemma 4.8 (Closedness of bounded terminal gains).

Let (Hn)(H^{n}) be SS-admissible strategies such that GTn=∫0THsn​d​SsG^{n}_{T}=\int_{0}^{T}H^{n}_{s}\,dS_{s} are bounded from below and converge in probability to a bounded random variable GTG_{T}. Then there exists an SS-admissible strategy HH such that GT=∫0THs​d​SsG_{T}=\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\,dS_{s}.

Proof.

The proof is the semimartingale closedness argument of Delbaen and Schachermayer (1994), with the topology of Emery (1979) and the stability result of Mémin (1980). Since SS is a continuous stochastic exponential with quadratic variation

⟨S⟩t=∫0tSs2​ξs2​𝑑s,\langle S\rangle_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}S_{s}^{2}\xi_{s}^{2}\,ds,

the admissibility condition is precisely H∈L2​(S)H\in L^{2}(S) locally. A sequence of terminal gains bounded from below has a Fatou-convergent subsequence in the semimartingale topology. The Emery-closedness of stochastic integrals yields a predictable limit integrand HH, and the lower bound prevents mass from escaping through doubling strategies. The Brownian representation on ℱW^=ℱW\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}=\mathcal{F}^{W} ensures that no additional orthogonal martingale component appears in the limit. ∎

Corollary 4.9 (Existence of a separating density).

If NFLVR holds on ℱW^\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}, then there exists a strictly positive ZT∈L1​(ℱTW^,ℙ)Z_{T}\in L^{1}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{P}) with 𝔼​ZT=1\mathbb{E}Z_{T}=1 such that SS is a local martingale under d​ℚ=ZT​d​ℙd\mathbb{Q}=Z_{T}d\mathbb{P}.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.8, the cone 𝒞\mathcal{C} is weak-star closed after intersection with L∞L^{\infty}. Kreps–Yan separation gives a strictly positive element of the predual that separates 𝒞\mathcal{C} from L+∞∖{0}L^{\infty}_{+}\setminus\{0\}. Normalising the separating functional gives ZTZ_{T}. The usual localisation argument then gives the local-martingale property of SS under ℚ\mathbb{Q}. ∎

4.7 Transform derivation at finite level

For N<∞N<\infty let W^(N)=π≤N​W^\widehat{W}^{(N)}=\pi_{\leq N}\widehat{W} and let ℓ(N)=π≤N​ℓ\ell^{(N)}=\pi_{\leq N}\ell. On the finite-dimensional coordinate vector Yt(N)=(⟨eI,W^t⟩)|I|≤NY^{(N)}_{t}=(\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle)_{|I|\leq N}, the Stratonovich-to-Itô conversion gives a polynomial semimartingale system

d​Yt(N)=bN​(Yt(N))​d​t+∑j=0dσN,j​(Yt(N))​d​Wtj,dY^{(N)}_{t}=b_{N}(Y^{(N)}_{t})\,dt+\sum_{j=0}^{d}\sigma_{N,j}(Y^{(N)}_{t})\,dW^{j}_{t},

where Wt0=tW^{0}_{t}=t is the time coordinate convention and each coefficient is polynomial in the signature coordinates. For uu finitely supported, set

Λt(N)​(u)=𝔼ℚ​[exp⁡{⟨u,W^T(N)⟩}∣ℱtW^].\Lambda_{t}^{(N)}(u)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left[\exp\{\left\langle u,\widehat{W}^{(N)}_{T}\right\rangle\}\mid\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{t}\right].

The affine-polynomial ansatz is

Λt(N)​(u)=exp⁡{⟨ψN​(T−t,u),W^t(N)⟩}.\Lambda_{t}^{(N)}(u)=\exp\{\left\langle\psi_{N}(T-t,u),\widehat{W}^{(N)}_{t}\right\rangle\}.

Applying Itô’s formula to the right-hand side and setting the drift equal to zero gives

∂τψN​(τ,u)=ℛN​(ψN​(τ,u)),ψN​(0,u)=u,\partial_{\tau}\psi_{N}(\tau,u)=\mathcal{R}_{N}(\psi_{N}(\tau,u)),\qquad\psi_{N}(0,u)=u,
