If τ≤T\tau\leq T is a stopping time, the stopped prolonged signature W^t∧τ\widehat{W}_{t\wedge\tau} is measurable with respect to ℱt∧τW\mathcal{F}^{W}_{t\wedge\tau}, and its first level recovers (t∧τ,Wt∧τ)(t\wedge\tau,W_{t\wedge\tau}). Hence

σ(W^s∧τ:s≤t)=σ(Ws∧τ:s≤t)\sigma(\widehat{W}_{s\wedge\tau}:s\leq t)=\sigma(W_{s\wedge\tau}:s\leq t)

after augmentation. This stopped version is used implicitly in localisation arguments for uniqueness and true-martingale upgrades.

Chen’s identity is compatible with stopping: for 0≤s≤t0\leq s\leq t,

W^0,t∧τ=W^0,s∧τ⊗W^s∧τ,t∧τ.\widehat{W}_{0,t\wedge\tau}=\widehat{W}_{0,s\wedge\tau}\otimes\widehat{W}_{s\wedge\tau,t\wedge\tau}.

The increment signature on the right is trivial when the stopping time has occurred before ss. Thus the algebraic multiplicativity of the signature is not lost under localisation.

Stratonovich–Itô conversion for signature coordinates

For a word I=(i1,…,in)I=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}) the Stratonovich coordinate ⟨eI,W^t⟩\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle is an iterated Stratonovich integral. Rewriting it in Itô form gives a finite sum indexed by contractions of adjacent equal Brownian letters. Schematically,

∫0<t1<⋯<tn<t∘dW^i1t1⋯∘dW^intn=∑Γ⊂{1,…,n−1}cΓ∫Δn−2​|Γ|​(t)dW^JΓdt|Γ|,\int_{0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}<t}\circ d\widehat{W}^{i_{1}}_{t_{1}}\cdots\circ d\widehat{W}^{i_{n}}_{t_{n}}=\sum_{\Gamma\subset\{1,\ldots,n-1\}}c_{\Gamma}\int_{\Delta_{n-2|\Gamma|}(t)}d\widehat{W}^{J_{\Gamma}}\,dt^{|\Gamma|},

where Γ\Gamma runs over non-overlapping bracket contractions and JΓJ_{\Gamma} is the word obtained after deleting the paired Brownian letters. The exact constants are powers of 1/21/2 from the Stratonovich correction. This finite expansion proves that every coordinate is a special semimartingale and that the finite-variation part is built from lower-order coordinates.

This conversion is used in Lemma 4.1. It is important that the operation is finite for each fixed word. Infinite-dimensional issues enter only after summing over all words with a weight. Therefore the special-semimartingale property of a fixed coordinate is independent of H1, while the simultaneous L2L^{2} control of all coordinates through the parameter ℓ\ell uses H1.

Lemma A.6 (Measure transport of signature moments).

Let ZT=d​ℚ/d​ℙZ_{T}=d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P} satisfy ZT∈Lr​(ℙ)Z_{T}\in L^{r}(\mathbb{P}) for some r>1r>1. If YY is a finite terminal signature polynomial with Y∈Lp​(ℙ)Y\in L^{p}(\mathbb{P}) for every p<∞p<\infty, then Y∈Lq​(ℚ)Y\in L^{q}(\mathbb{Q}) for every finite qq satisfying q​r/(r−1)<∞qr/(r-1)<\infty.

Proof.

By Hölder,

𝔼ℚ​|Y|q=𝔼ℙ​[ZT​|Y|q]≤‖ZT‖Lr​(ℙ)​(𝔼ℙ​|Y|q​r/(r−1))(r−1)/r.\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left\lvert Y\right\rvert^{q}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[Z_{T}\left\lvert Y\right\rvert^{q}]\leq\left\lVert Z_{T}\right\rVert_{L^{r}(\mathbb{P})}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\left\lvert Y\right\rvert^{qr/(r-1)}\right)^{(r-1)/r}.

The final factor is finite by the Brownian signature moment estimate and the fact that YY is a finite polynomial in terminal signature coordinates. ∎

Lemma A.7 (Uniform moment bound for finite truncations).

Let ww satisfy H2 and w⁡(n)≤rnw(n)\leq r^{n}. Then for every p<∞p<\infty,

supN≥0𝔼​supt≤T‖π≤N​W^t‖wp<∞.\sup_{N\geq 0}\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lVert\pi_{\leq N}\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{w}^{p}<\infty.
Proof.

The projection cannot increase the weighted norm. Hence

‖π≤N​W^t‖w≤‖W^t‖w.\left\lVert\pi_{\leq N}\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{w}\leq\left\lVert\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rVert_{w}.

The supremum over tt is handled by applying the Brownian rough-path moment estimate on dyadic partitions and using the continuity of the Stratonovich signature. The factorial decay in the level beats the exponential growth of the weight. This gives a finite bound independent of NN. ∎

Lemma A.8 (Continuity of conditional projection).

Let XN→XX_{N}\to X in L2​(ℱTW^,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{Q}). Then

𝔼ℚ​[XN∣ℱTS]→𝔼ℚ​[X∣ℱTS]in ​L2​(ℱTS,ℚ).\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{N}\mid\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T}]\to\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X\mid\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T}]\quad\hbox{in }L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}).
Proof.

Conditional expectation is the orthogonal projection from L2​(ℱTW^,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{\widehat{W}}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) onto the closed subspace L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}). Orthogonal projections have operator norm one. Therefore

‖𝔼ℚ​[XN−X∣ℱTS]‖L2​(ℚ)≤‖XN−X‖L2​(ℚ)→0.\left\lVert\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{N}-X\mid\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T}]\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{Q})}\leq\left\lVert X_{N}-X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{Q})}\to 0.

This is the mechanism behind the price-filtration restrictions in Theorems 5.3 and 6.3. ∎

Auxiliary Brownian estimates

For later reference, the Brownian signature moment bound also implies a tail estimate. If w⁡(n)=rnw(n)=r^{n} and RN​(t)=π>N​W^tR_{N}(t)=\pi_{>N}\widehat{W}_{t}, then for every p<∞p<\infty there are constants C,c>0C,c>0 such that

𝔼​supt≤T‖RN​(t)‖wp≤C​∑n>N(c​r​T)p​n(n!)p/2.\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}\left\lVert R_{N}(t)\right\rVert_{w}^{p}\leq C\sum_{n>N}\frac{(cr\sqrt{T})^{pn}}{(n!)^{p/2}}.

The right-hand side decays faster than exponentially in NN along fixed TT and rr. This estimate is stronger than the abstract weight-tail bound used in the hedging theorem. It is not used in the main statements because the latter are formulated for general admissible weights, but it explains the fast numerical convergence observed in finite-signature implementations.

Appendix B The infinite-dimensional Riccati equation

The coordinate form of the Riccati operator is

ℛ​(u)I=∑JbJI​(ℓ)​uJ+12​∑J,KΓJ,KI​(ℓ)​uJ​uK,|I|≥0,\mathcal{R}(u)_{I}=\sum_{J}b_{J}^{I}(\ell)u_{J}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{J,K}\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell)u_{J}u_{K},\qquad|I|\geq 0, (1)

where the sums are finite on each finite truncation and the coefficients bJI​(ℓ)b_{J}^{I}(\ell) and ΓJ,KI​(ℓ)\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell) are defined by the generator and carre-du-champ identities in Definition 2.18. In particular, the coefficient of the quadratic term is a structural constant attached to the input pair (J,K)(J,K) and output word II. It is not the output-only scalar ⟨ℓ⊔⁣⊔ℓ,eI⟩\left\langle\ell\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}\ell,e_{I}\right\rangle repeated over all shuffle pairs.

Lemma B.1 (Shuffle product estimate).

Assume H2. There is a constant Cw⊔⁣⊔C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}} such that

‖a⊔⁣⊔b‖w≤Cw⊔⁣⊔​‖a‖w​‖b‖w,a,b∈Tw.\left\lVert a\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}b\right\rVert_{w}\leq C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{w},\qquad a,b\in T_{w}.
Proof.

At level nn, the shuffle product is the sum of all order-preserving interlacings of levels kk and n−kn-k. The number of such interlacings is bounded by 2n2^{n}. The exponential upper bound in H2 absorbs this combinatorial factor after replacing the weight constant by an equivalent one, and the submultiplicative estimate then gives the same convolution bound as for concatenation. This proves continuity of the shuffle product on the weighted algebra used in the Riccati proof. ∎

Lemma B.2 (Local Lipschitz estimate).

The operator ℛ\mathcal{R} is locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of TwT_{w}.

Proof.

Write ℛ⁡(u)=L⁡(u)+12​B​(u,u)\mathcal{R}(u)=L(u)+\tfrac{1}{2}B(u,u), where

L​(u)I=∑JbJI​(ℓ)​uJ,B​(u,v)I=∑J,KΓJ,KI​(ℓ)​uJ​vKL(u)_{I}=\sum_{J}b_{J}^{I}(\ell)u_{J},\qquad B(u,v)_{I}=\sum_{J,K}\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell)\,u_{J}v_{K}

are, respectively, the generator drift (linear) and the carre-du-champ (bilinear) parts of Definition 2.18. The quadratic part is the bilinear form BB evaluated on the diagonal; it is not the shuffle square u⊔⁣⊔uu\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}u. The shuffle product enters only as the tool that controls the convolution structure of BB in the weighted norm.

Boundedness of BB. On each finite truncation the structural constants ΓJ,KI​(ℓ)\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell) are produced by the carre-du-champ of the generator 𝒜Nℓ\mathcal{A}_{N}^{\ell}, hence are finite linear combinations of the components of ℓ\ell paired with shuffle-Hopf structure constants ⟨eJ⊔⁣⊔eK,eI⟩\left\langle e_{J}\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}e_{K},e_{I}\right\rangle. Consequently there is a constant Λ⁡(ℓ,w)<∞\Lambda(\ell,w)<\infty such that, level by level,

∑Iw⁡(|I|)​|∑J,KΓJ,KI​(ℓ)​aJ​bK|≤Λ⁡(ℓ,w)​Cw⊔⁣⊔​‖a‖w​‖b‖w,\sum_{I}w(|I|)\,\Big|\sum_{J,K}\Gamma^{I}_{J,K}(\ell)\,a_{J}b_{K}\Big|\leq\Lambda(\ell,w)\,C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}\,\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}\,\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{w},

where Cw⊔⁣⊔C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}} is the shuffle Banach-algebra constant of Lemma B.1 and the bound uses that the support of ΓJ,KI\Gamma^{I}_{J,K} in (J,K)(J,K) for fixed II is contained in the shuffle-pair set of eIe_{I}, so the double sum is dominated by the weighted shuffle convolution ‖a⊔⁣⊔b‖w\left\lVert a\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}b\right\rVert_{w}. Hence B:Tw×Tw→TwB:T_{w}\times T_{w}\to T_{w} is a bounded symmetric bilinear map with ‖B⁡(a,b)‖w≤Λ⁡(ℓ,w)​Cw⊔⁣⊔​‖a‖w​‖b‖w\left\lVert B(a,b)\right\rVert_{w}\leq\Lambda(\ell,w)C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{w}\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{w}.

Lipschitz estimate. The drift LL is a bounded linear operator, ‖L⁡(u)−L⁡(v)‖w≤‖L‖​‖u−v‖w\left\lVert L(u)-L(v)\right\rVert_{w}\leq\left\lVert L\right\rVert\,\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{w} with ‖L‖≤Λ⁡(ℓ,w)\left\lVert L\right\rVert\leq\Lambda(\ell,w). For the quadratic part, polarisation gives

B⁡(u,u)−B⁡(v,v)=B⁡(u−v,u)+B⁡(v,u−v),B(u,u)-B(v,v)=B(u-v,u)+B(v,u-v),

so that, for u,vu,v in the ball of radius RR,

‖B⁡(u,u)−B⁡(v,v)‖w≤Λ⁡(ℓ,w)​Cw⊔⁣⊔​(‖u‖w+‖v‖w)​‖u−v‖w≤2​R​Λ​(ℓ,w)​Cw⊔⁣⊔​‖u−v‖w.\left\lVert B(u,u)-B(v,v)\right\rVert_{w}\leq\Lambda(\ell,w)C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}\big(\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{w}+\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{w}\big)\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{w}\leq 2R\,\Lambda(\ell,w)C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}\,\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{w}.

Combining the two parts,

‖ℛ⁡(u)−ℛ⁡(v)‖w≤C⁡(R,w,ℓ)​‖u−v‖w,C⁡(R,w,ℓ):=Λ⁡(ℓ,w)​(1+R​Cw⊔⁣⊔),\left\lVert\mathcal{R}(u)-\mathcal{R}(v)\right\rVert_{w}\leq C(R,w,\ell)\,\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{w},\qquad C(R,w,\ell):=\Lambda(\ell,w)\big(1+R\,C_{w}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}\big),

a finite local constant. The estimate is uniform on bounded sets and passes to the weighted projective limit because the truncated operators ℛN\mathcal{R}_{N} are consistent (degree-respecting), so the bound is independent of the truncation level. ∎

Lemma B.3 (Continuity of the flow).

The flow u0↦utu_{0}\mapsto u_{t} defined by ∂tut=ℛ⁡(ut)\partial_{t}u_{t}=\mathcal{R}(u_{t}) is continuous on its domain of existence.

Proof.

For two solutions uu and vv started from u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} in a common local-existence ball, the local Lipschitz estimate gives

‖ut−vt‖w≤‖u0−v0‖w+C​∫0t‖us−vs‖w​𝑑s.\left\lVert u_{t}-v_{t}\right\rVert_{w}\leq\left\lVert u_{0}-v_{0}\right\rVert_{w}+C\int_{0}^{t}\left\lVert u_{s}-v_{s}\right\rVert_{w}\,ds.

Gronwall’s lemma gives the stated continuity. ∎

Lemma B.4 (Finite-dimensional Riccati comparison).

Let yy solve y˙=a​y2−b​y−c\dot{y}=ay^{2}-by-c on an interval with a>0a>0 and b,c≥0b,c\geq 0. For every horizon T>0T>0 there exists y0y_{0} large enough such that the solution with y⁡(0)=y0y(0)=y_{0} explodes before TT.

Proof.

Choose y0y_{0} so large that a​y2−b​y−c≥(a/2)​y2ay^{2}-by-c\geq(a/2)y^{2} for y≥y0/2y\geq y_{0}/2. The comparison equation z˙=(a/2)​z2\dot{z}=(a/2)z^{2}, z⁡(0)=y0z(0)=y_{0}, explodes at time 2/(a​y0)2/(ay_{0}). Taking y0>2/(a​T)y_{0}>2/(aT) gives explosion before TT for the comparison equation and therefore for yy as long as the solution stays above the threshold. The derivative is positive at y0y_{0}, so it does. ∎

Lemma B.5 (Quotient Hilbert projection).

Let HH be a closed subspace of a Hilbert space LL and let V⊂L/HV\subset L/H be a closed subspace of the quotient. Every class [X]∈L/H[X]\in L/H has a unique orthogonal projection onto VV.

Proof.

The quotient by a closed subspace is a Hilbert space with norm ‖[X]‖=infY∈H‖X−Y‖\left\lVert[X]\right\rVert=\inf_{Y\in H}\left\lVert X-Y\right\rVert. The result is the ordinary Hilbert projection theorem applied in that quotient. This is the formal setting of Lemma 6.1 and Theorem 6.3. ∎

Comparison principle for scalar Riccati projections

Let yy solve

y˙t=a​yt2+b​yt+c,a>0,\dot{y}_{t}=ay_{t}^{2}+by_{t}+c,\qquad a>0,

with initial value y0>0y_{0}>0. If yty_{t} remains positive, then for every interval on which a​yt2+b​yt+c≥(a/2)​yt2ay_{t}^{2}+by_{t}+c\geq(a/2)y_{t}^{2} one has

y˙t≥a2​yt2,\dot{y}_{t}\geq\frac{a}{2}y_{t}^{2},

and therefore

1yt≤1y0−a2​t.\frac{1}{y_{t}}\leq\frac{1}{y_{0}}-\frac{a}{2}t.

Thus yy explodes no later than 2/(a​y0)2/(ay_{0}) after it enters that region. This elementary comparison is the scalar argument required when a model-specific Riccati coordinate actually satisfies a self-quadratic lower bound. The finite-dimensional subsystem need not be exactly scalar; it is enough that one coordinate dominates a scalar Riccati equation with positive quadratic coefficient after the remaining coordinates are controlled on a short interval.

Lemma B.6 (Short-time domination for finite Riccati subsystems).

Consider a finite-dimensional Riccati system whose kkth coordinate satisfies

y˙k=a​yj2+L⁡(y),a>0,\dot{y}_{k}=ay_{j}^{2}+L(y),\qquad a>0,

where LL is affine on bounded sets. There are initial conditions in the finite-dimensional state space for which the solution explodes before any prescribed horizon T>0T>0.

Proof.

Choose the initial value of the active quadratic coordinate large and the remaining coordinates bounded. On a short interval the affine term is dominated by half of the positive quadratic term. The preceding scalar comparison gives an explosion time bounded by a constant multiple of the reciprocal initial size. Taking the initial size sufficiently large places the explosion before TT. ∎

Consistency of projected Riccati equations

For N≥0N\geq 0 let πN\pi_{N} be the projection onto words of length at most NN. The projected vector field is

ℛN​(u):=πN​ℛ​(πN​u).\mathcal{R}_{N}(u):=\pi_{N}\mathcal{R}(\pi_{N}u).

Because the shuffle product respects degree, the coordinate ℛ​(u)I\mathcal{R}(u)_{I} depends only on coordinates uJu_{J} with |J|≤|I||J|\leq|I|. Hence

πM​ℛN​(u)=ℛM​(πM​u),M≤N,\pi_{M}\mathcal{R}_{N}(u)=\mathcal{R}_{M}(\pi_{M}u),\qquad M\leq N,

whenever uu is supported in levels at most NN. This compatibility is the projective-system structure behind the passage from finite transforms to the weighted Riccati equation.

Finite-dimensional projections of the Riccati equation

Let ℛN=π≤N​ℛ​π≤N\mathcal{R}_{N}=\pi_{\leq N}\mathcal{R}\pi_{\leq N}. Since π≤N​Tw\pi_{\leq N}T_{w} is finite-dimensional, the equation

u˙tN=ℛN​(utN),u0N=π≤N​u0,\dot{u}^{N}_{t}=\mathcal{R}_{N}(u^{N}_{t}),\qquad u^{N}_{0}=\pi_{\leq N}u_{0},

has a unique maximal classical solution. The maximal time is characterised by the usual explosion criterion: either the solution exists on the whole interval or ‖utN‖w→∞\left\lVert u^{N}_{t}\right\rVert_{w}\to\infty as tt approaches the lifetime. This finite-dimensional criterion is the correct tool for model-specific transform-explosion checks; no three-coordinate comparison is invoked in the main text.

The finite projections are compatible with the full vector field on bounded sets. If uu is supported in levels at most NN and M≥2​N+deg⁡ℓM\geq 2N+\deg\ell, then the level-≤N\leq N coordinates of ℛM​(u)\mathcal{R}_{M}(u) agree with those of ℛ⁡(u)\mathcal{R}(u). The factor 2​N2N comes from the shuffle square u⊔⁣⊔uu\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}u. Thus finite systems approximate the full system in a triangular way: low levels close after including enough higher levels to absorb the shuffle product.

Lemma B.7 (Boundedness criterion for global solvability).

Let uu solve u˙t=ℛ⁡(ut)\dot{u}_{t}=\mathcal{R}(u_{t}) on its maximal interval [0,τ)[0,\tau). If supt<τ‖ut‖w<∞\sup_{t<\tau}\left\lVert u_{t}\right\rVert_{w}<\infty, then τ\tau is not finite.

Proof.

The local Lipschitz estimate in Appendix B gives a local existence time depending only on the radius of the ball containing the solution. If the solution remains in a bounded ball up to τ\tau, it can be restarted at times approaching τ\tau with a uniform positive existence time. This contradicts maximality of a finite lifetime. ∎

Lemma B.8 (Comparison on positive cones).

Assume that, on a finite coordinate subsystem, the vector field satisfies

y˙i≥Fi​(y),\dot{y}_{i}\geq F_{i}(y),

where FF is locally Lipschitz and order-preserving on the positive cone. If zz solves z˙=F⁡(z)\dot{z}=F(z) with z⁡(0)≤y⁡(0)z(0)\leq y(0), then z⁡(t)≤y⁡(t)z(t)\leq y(t) up to the first exit time from the cone.

Proof.

This is the standard quasimonotone comparison theorem for finite-dimensional ODEs. Apply it to (y−z)+(y-z)_{+} after smoothing the positive part, or equivalently use the first-contact argument: at the first coordinate where equality could fail, quasimonotonicity prevents the derivative of yi−ziy_{i}-z_{i} from becoming negative. ∎

Normalisation of the shuffle coefficient

The coefficient convention in equation (1) is fixed through the generator and the carre-du-champ, not by inserting an output-only shuffle coefficient into every input pair. In the pure signature state, the empty-word coordinate is constant and has zero generator. In the price-extended Black–Scholes state Xt=log⁡StX_{t}=\log S_{t}, however,

d​Xt=−12​σ2​d​t+σ​d​Bt,dX_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}dt+\sigma dB_{t},

so the exponential-affine transform exp⁡{u​Xt+ϕ⁡(T−t,u)}\exp\{uX_{t}+\phi(T-t,u)\} satisfies

∂τϕ=12​σ2​u2−12​σ2​u.\partial_{\tau}\phi=\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}u.

This is the scalar Black–Scholes normalisation relevant for the price-extended transform. It also explains why the pure signature empty word should not be treated as a non-constant log-price coordinate.

For a first-level Brownian parameter ℓ=a​e1\ell=ae_{1}, the shuffle identity gives e1⊔⁣⊔e1=2​e11e_{1}\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}e_{1}=2e_{11}. The corresponding quadratic coefficient at level two is obtained from the carre-du-champ structural constant of the finite generator. This fixes the factor of two without invoking an unrestricted sum over all pairs whose shuffle merely contains the output word.

Riccati explosion and transform failure

The finite-time blow-up of a Riccati coordinate has a direct transform interpretation. If ψ⁡(τ,u)\psi(\tau,u) explodes at τ∗<T\tau^{\ast}<T, then the exponential-affine candidate

exp⁡{⟨ψ⁡(T−t,u),W^t⟩}\exp\{\left\langle\psi(T-t,u),\widehat{W}_{t}\right\rangle\}

ceases to be finite before the terminal time. Therefore the conditional transform cannot be represented globally by the Riccati flow for that initial condition. The transform implication is used only after a finite-dimensional Riccati subsystem has been verified to have a finite lifetime. The paper no longer infers such a lifetime from the bounded sine example.

The argument is local in the finite-dimensional subsystem. It does not require proving explosion of every coordinate of the infinite equation. A finite projection proves failure of global solvability only when its coordinates satisfy a genuine self-quadratic comparison or when an external moment-explosion theorem applies. A positive off-diagonal quadratic term alone is not enough.

Global solutions and transform domains

The Riccati flow is naturally defined on a domain of initial data rather than on the whole Banach algebra. For a fixed horizon TT, define

𝒰T:={u0∈Tw:the solution of u˙t=ℛ(ut),u(0)=u0, exists on [0,T]}.\mathcal{U}_{T}:=\{u_{0}\in T_{w}:\hbox{the solution of }\dot{u}_{t}=\mathcal{R}(u_{t}),\ u(0)=u_{0},\hbox{ exists on }[0,T]\}.

Theorem 4.2 assumes that 𝒟fin⊂𝒰T\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fin}}\subset\mathcal{U}_{T}. This is the transform-domain version of absence of moment explosion. The set 𝒰T\mathcal{U}_{T} is open by local well-posedness and continuous dependence. It is generally not treated as all of TwT_{w} without a model-specific transform-explosion analysis; the main text deliberately keeps this as a separate transform-domain condition.

The transform domain shrinks as TT grows. If T1<T2T_{1}<T_{2}, then 𝒰T2⊂𝒰T1\mathcal{U}_{T_{2}}\subset\mathcal{U}_{T_{1}}. In affine volatility models this monotonicity is the familiar monotonicity of moment-explosion times. In the signature setting it becomes a statement about the lifetime of an infinite-dimensional generator/carre-du-champ quadratic flow.

Appendix C The Galtchouk–Kunita–Watanabe projection

Theorem C.1 (Galtchouk–Kunita–Watanabe projection).

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a closed subspace of L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) and let X∈L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)X\in L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}). There exists a unique Xℋ∈ℋX_{\mathcal{H}}\in\mathcal{H} such that X−Xℋ⟂ℋX-X_{\mathcal{H}}\perp\mathcal{H}.

Proof.

This is the Hilbert projection theorem applied to the closed subspace ℋ\mathcal{H}. The martingale version used for stochastic integrals is the Galtchouk–Kunita–Watanabe decomposition; see Kunita and Watanabe (1967) and Föllmer and Schweizer (1991). ∎

Theorem C.2 (Orthogonal complement on the price filtration).

For the price filtration ℱTS\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T}, the L2​(ℚ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q})-orthogonal complement of stochastic integrals against SS on [0,T][0,T] equals the L2​(ℚ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q})-closure of the linear span of terminal signature coordinates {⟨eI,W^T⟩:|I|>NS∗}\{\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{T}\right\rangle:|I|>N^{\ast}_{S}\}, viewed modulo elements of L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) that are themselves representable as stochastic integrals against SS.

Proof.

The signature uniqueness theorem embeds ℱTS\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T} into the Brownian path sigma-field recovered from the terminal signature. The GKW projection splits L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) into the closed subspace of stochastic integrals against SS and its orthogonal complement. By the definition of NS∗N^{\ast}_{S}, the depth-≤NS∗\leq N^{\ast}_{S} coordinates are precisely those captured by the static completion, while the surviving depth->NS∗>N^{\ast}_{S} coordinates represent the residual quotient directions. This gives the stated description. ∎

Hilbert-space proof of quotient positivity

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a Hilbert space, ℋ0⊂ℋ\mathcal{H}_{0}\subset\mathcal{H} a closed subspace, and q:ℋ→ℋ/ℋ0q:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}/\mathcal{H}_{0} the quotient map identified with the orthogonal complement ℋ0⟂\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}. For vectors Y1,…,Ym∈ℋY_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}\in\mathcal{H}, the quotient Gram matrix is

G~i​j=⟨q​Yi,q​Yj⟩ℋ/ℋ0.\widetilde{G}_{ij}=\left\langle qY_{i},qY_{j}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}/\mathcal{H}_{0}}.

It is positive definite if and only if q​Y1,…,q​YmqY_{1},\ldots,qY_{m} are linearly independent. This elementary fact is the Hilbert-space core of Lemma 6.1. In the application, ℋ=L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) and ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is the stochastic-integral subspace.

Proof.

For any vector a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

a⊤​G~​a=‖∑i=1mai​q​Yi‖ℋ/ℋ02.a^{\top}\widetilde{G}a=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}qY_{i}\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}/\mathcal{H}_{0}}^{2}.

This quantity is strictly positive for every non-zero aa exactly when the quotient classes are linearly independent. Symmetry and positive semidefiniteness are immediate from the inner product. ∎

Projection error and closure

Let (𝒱m)m(\mathcal{V}_{m})_{m} be an increasing sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces of a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, and let Πm\Pi_{m} be the orthogonal projection onto 𝒱m\mathcal{V}_{m}. If 𝒱=∪m𝒱m¯\mathcal{V}=\overline{\cup_{m}\mathcal{V}_{m}}, then

Πm​X→Π𝒱​Xin ​ℋ.\Pi_{m}X\to\Pi_{\mathcal{V}}X\qquad\text{in }\mathcal{H}.

This standard result is the closure statement used in the residual expansion. It also justifies computing the coefficients through finite Gram matrices: each finite system gives the projection onto one finite truncation, and the projections converge to the projection onto the closed residual span.

Process form of the GKW decomposition

Let X∈L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)X\in L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}) and set MtX=𝔼ℚ​[X∣ℱtS]M^{X}_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X\mid\mathcal{F}^{S}_{t}]. The GKW decomposition with respect to the square-integrable martingale part of SS gives

MtX=M0X+∫0tHs​d​Ss+Lt,M^{X}_{t}=M^{X}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}H_{s}\,dS_{s}+L_{t},

where LL is a square-integrable martingale orthogonal to SS. Taking terminal values gives Theorem 6.3. The residual is LTL_{T}. Orthogonality of martingales implies orthogonality of terminal variables:

𝔼ℚ​[LT​∫0TGs​d​Ss]=0\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left[L_{T}\int_{0}^{T}G_{s}\,dS_{s}\right]=0

for every admissible GG. Conversely, terminal orthogonality for every GG gives strong orthogonality of the martingales after localisation.

Lemma C.3 (Closedness of stochastic integrals in L2L^{2}).

The set

{∫0THs​d​Ss:𝔼ℚ​∫0THs2​d​⟨S⟩s<∞}\left\{\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\,dS_{s}:\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}^{2}\,d\langle S\rangle_{s}<\infty\right\}

is a closed subspace of L2​(ℱTS,ℚ)L^{2}(\mathcal{F}^{S}_{T},\mathbb{Q}).

Proof.

The map H↦∫0THs​d​SsH\mapsto\int_{0}^{T}H_{s}\,dS_{s} is an isometry from the Hilbert space L2​(d⁡⟨S⟩⊗d​ℚ)L^{2}(d\langle S\rangle\otimes d\mathbb{Q}) modulo null integrands into L2​(ℚ)L^{2}(\mathbb{Q}) after centring. The range of an isometry is closed. ∎

Finite truncation algorithm for the projection

For a truncation set ℐm\mathcal{I}_{m}, the projection calculation has four algebraic steps. First compute the terminal coordinates YI=⟨eI,W^T⟩Y_{I}=\left\langle e_{I},\widehat{W}_{T}\right\rangle for I∈ℐmI\in\mathcal{I}_{m}. Second remove the stochastic-integral component by replacing each YIY_{I} by YI−Πℋ0​YIY_{I}-\Pi_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Y_{I}. Third form the quotient Gram matrix. Fourth solve the finite normal equations. The limiting theorem says that, as mm increases, the projected residual converges in L2L^{2}.

This is not presented as a numerical algorithm in the main theorem because the conditioning of the Gram matrix is model-dependent. The mathematical statement is the convergence and uniqueness of the projection, not a claim about numerical stability. In applications, regularisation of the finite Gram system may be necessary, but it does not alter the Hilbert-space decomposition.

Quotient Gram matrices

Let Y1,…,YmY_{1},\ldots,Y_{m} be terminal signature coordinates above the completeness depth, and let ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} be the stochastic-integral subspace. The quotient Gram matrix is

G~i​j=⟨[Yi],[Yj]⟩L2/ℋ0=⟨Yi−Πℋ0​Yi,Yj−Πℋ0​Yj⟩L2.\widetilde{G}_{ij}=\left\langle[Y_{i}],[Y_{j}]\right\rangle_{L^{2}/\mathcal{H}_{0}}=\left\langle Y_{i}-\Pi_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Y_{i},Y_{j}-\Pi_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Y_{j}\right\rangle_{L^{2}}.

This is the matrix that is positive definite in Lemma 6.1. The raw matrix Gi​j=𝔼ℚ​[Yi​Yj]G_{ij}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[Y_{i}Y_{j}] can be singular because two different signature coordinates may have the same projection onto the price filtration or may differ by a stochastic integral against SS. The quotient formulation removes exactly those null directions.

Lemma C.4 (Equivalence of raw and quotient normal equations).

If the coordinate family has already been reduced by removing all vectors whose quotient class is zero and by choosing one representative from each quotient-linear-dependence class, then the raw normal equations and the quotient normal equations have the same solution.

Proof.

On the reduced family, each representative is orthogonal to the null directions by construction. Replacing YiY_{i} by Yi−Πℋ0​YiY_{i}-\Pi_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Y_{i} changes neither the residual projection nor the right-hand side against the GKW residual, because the residual is orthogonal to ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. Therefore the coefficient system is unchanged. ∎

Residual tail as model-risk statistic

The bound

‖RT‖L2​(ℚ)≤κ⁡(w,NS∗)​‖X‖L2​(ℚ)\left\lVert R_{T}\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{Q})}\leq\kappa(w,N_{S}^{\ast})\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{Q})}

turns the weight into a model-risk statistic. If two calibrated signature-volatility models fit the same liquid option surface but have different admissible weights, the one with faster decay of κ⁡(w,N)\kappa(w,N) has a smaller structural bound on unspanned high-depth claims. This is not a calibration statement; it is a theorem-level stability statement inside the Hilbert space of terminal payoffs.

The estimate is deliberately conservative. It ignores the smallest eigenvalue of the finite Gram matrix, the actual coefficient decay of the payoff, and any special symmetry of the model. In numerical implementations those features can reduce the observed residual substantially. The theorem keeps only the part that is invariant under coordinate choices: the weight tail beyond the completeness depth.

Static completion and dynamic projection

The static and dynamic components of the completed market play different roles. The dynamic projection handles the martingale part spanned by SS. The static option strip inserts terminal payoff directions that cannot be spanned dynamically because the volatility factor is hidden from the price filtration. The signature coordinates organise the static directions by tensor degree. This is why Theorem 5.3 and Theorem 6.3 are paired: the first identifies how many low-degree directions must be inserted; the second measures the high-degree directions left outside the insertion.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
